articles.title: 1,854 Zambales residents flee homes anew as heavy rains continue
articles.summary: SAN ANTONIO, Zambales — Heavy rains prompted the evacuation of 604 Zambales families, or 1,854 residents, on Monday. Data from the Zambales Provincial Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office…

blocks.text: SAN ANTONIO, Zambales — Heavy rains prompted the evacuation of 604 Zambales families, or 1,854 residents, on Monday.

Data from the Zambales Provincial Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office showed that 261 families 899 individuals) from five towns in the province have taken shelter inside evacuation centers as of 3:00 p.m. on Monday
Another 343 families (955 individuals) sought temporary shelter elsewhere.
Among those staying in evacuation centers, Castillejos town had the highest number, with 145 families (512 individuals), followed by Cabangan town with 66 families (or 206 individuals).
The municipality of San Marcelino recorded 18 families (50 individuals), while Subic town had 20 families 83 individuals). San Antonio town had 12 families 48 individuals).
The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) warned of continued heavy rainfall due to the southwest monsoon.
The weather bureau forecast 50 to 100 millimeters of rain in Zambales from Monday to Thursday noon (Sept. 10). /coa

blocks.text: The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao is holding its first parliamentary elections on September 14, 2026, after being postponed at least four times: first in May 2022, then in May 2025, October 2025, and again in March 2026.

The historic polls are seen as a pivotal moment in the decades-long peace process in a region that was mired in conflict and socioeconomic and political challenges. The upcoming elections are also a test for the Bangsamoro transition and the institutions and systems established in the last seven years.

articles.title: ICC prosecution asks to include prior testimony of witness in Rodrigo Duterte case
articles.summary: The Prosecution at the International Criminal Court asked the Chamber to admit into evidence the previously recorded testimony of a witness in the case against former president Rodrigo Duterte.

blocks.text: Published September 8, 2026 9:08am
The Prosecution at the International Criminal Court (ICC) asked the Chamber to admit into evidence the previously recorded testimony of a witness in the case against former president Rodrigo Duterte.
In a document dated September 7, the Prosecution asked permission to introduce the prior recorded testimony of witness P-1100 under Rule 68(3) of the ICC Rules of Procedure and Evidence.
The prosecution also asked to conduct a focused supplementary examination of the witness once he appears in court.

“Granting the request will enhance the expeditiousness of the proceedings by reducing the length of the witness’s direct examination from seven hours to two hours, thus saving at least five hours of court time,” the Prosecution said.
For the Prosecution, the said testimony is relevant to its allegations involving a policy to “neutralise” alleged criminals in the Philippines through violent crimes, including murder.

The testimony also provides evidence on the alleged modus operandi of the Davao Death Squad (DDS), as well as Duterte's alleged individual criminal responsibility, including his knowledge and intent, according to the Prosecution.
The trial is scheduled to begin on November 30, 2026.

Last April, the ICC confirmed the charges of crimes against humanity against former Duterte in connection with the killings during his war on drugs when he was mayor of Davao City and when he was president. —KG, GMA News

articles.title: Ukraine's chief prosecutor resigns over call centre corruption scandal
articles.summary: In his resignation letter, Ruslan Kravchenko denied the allegations against him, saying he did not want his office "to be used as a tool in political confrontation".

blocks.text: Ukraine's chief prosecutor Ruslan Kravchenko has resigned over corruption allegations related to illegal call centres in the country.
It follows a search of his offices over the weekend by Ukrainian anti-corruption investigators, who said they had identified a money-laundering scheme led by an official in Kravchenko's office.

In his resignation letter, Kravchenko said he did not want his position to be used as a "tool for political confrontation", and referenced an earlier post in which he rejected the claims as "unsubstantiated".
Corruption scandals have plagued Kyiv throughout the war against Russia, with accusations levelled at several members of President Volodymyr Zelensky's inner circle.

According to Ukraine's National Anti-Corruption Bureau (Nabu) and Specialised Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (Sap), the network in Kravchenko's office received money to protect call centres that carried out phone scams and "laundered millions in assets".
The money was then used to buy property, jewellery, and other valuables, according to Nabu.
Kravchenko released a statement on Sunday evening dismissing the allegations as "completely unsubstantiated", and denied any wrongdoing.
He tendered his resignation a day later, thanking Zelensky and the Ukrainian parliament for their "trust". The Ukrainian president is yet to comment publicly on the resignation.
Despite the creation of two Ukrainian anti-corruption bodies, Nabu and Sap, over a decade ago, corruption continues to be a significant problem in the country.
In 2025, nationwide protests broke out after Zelensky tried to implement reforms that would curb the independence of Nabu and Sap.
Kyiv's European partners expressed alarm at the announcement, with ambassadors from the G7 group of nations warning it could endanger Ukraine's integration into the European Union.
Ukraine is an EU candidate country, a status it was granted on condition it mounted a credible fight against corruption.
Zelensky reinstated the freedom of the two anti-corruption bodies as a result of the backlash, but questions have persisted over his commitment to anti-corruption reform.
Last month, Nabu said it had uncovered a scheme to misappropriate more than $3m (£2.2m) in Ukrainian currency to pay bail for a former energy minister accused of money laundering.
A senior official in Zelensky's office alleged to be involved was sacked.

articles.title: New prize named for late author Andrew Pyper will recognize horror and thriller writers
articles.summary: Heidi Pyper says she's frustrated that horror and thriller writers like her late husband, Andrew Pyper, don't get the recognition they deserve, noting that he wasn't considered for Canada's top…

image.caption: Heidi Pyper, left, is shown with her late husband, author Andrew Pyper. She says the Andrew Pyper Prize for Genre Fiction honours his legacy and will encourage other horror and thriller authors. (Submitted by Heidi Pyper)

blocks.text: The Current·New

Heidi Pyper says she's frustrated that horror and thriller writers like her late husband, Andrew Pyper, don't get the recognition they deserve, noting that he wasn't considered for Canada's top literary prizes because of the genre of his books. She hopes a new prize will help honour his legacy and encourage other writers.
Announcement of $20,000 award coincides with release of Pyper's final novel
LISTEN | New $20,000 literary prize created to honour Andrew Pyper's legacy:
The Current8:12A new writing prize honouring Andrew Pyper
Heidi Pyper says her late husband, Andrew, wasn't just a bestselling author. He was also generous, curious and truly cared about people.
Affectionately known as "Canada's Stephen King," Andrew died in January 2025 of complications from cancer at the age of 56.

He was a prolific and acclaimed writer of horror, thrillers and other types of speculative fiction, including The Killing Circle and The Demonologist, and Pyper said her husband wrote characters who had great depth.
But she said she's frustrated that writers like Andrew don't get the recognition they deserve, noting there aren't many genre-specific awards available for horror or thriller writing.
That's why Andrew's friend and fellow author, Craig Davidson, helped create the Andrew Pyper Prize for Genre Fiction.

items: Acclaimed thriller writer Andrew Pyper dead at age 56

blocks.text: The $20,000 prize will be administered through the Writers’ Trust of Canada. To be eligible to win, writers must have published at least three books in the horror, thriller or speculative fiction genre. Thanks to a massive campaign, enough money has been raised to support the prize for seven years.
The announcement for the award coincides with the release of Andrew's final novel, Driven.
As a reader and writer of horror, he believed that the genre could expand people’s understanding of the human condition.
Pyper said she hopes the prize will help support and encourage authors like Andrew. She spoke to Matt Galloway, host of The Current, about the prize and legacy she wants it to leave.
When you listen to Andrew talk about horror and the human condition, what's going through your mind?

It brings such a smile to my face hearing Andrew talk about horror, thriller and genre writing in a way that's deep and meaningful because he brought a lot of depth to his writing. Particularly with the characters that he put under great duress. I remember my dad reading The Wildfire Season and saying, "Why does he keep putting these people I care about in such jeopardy?" And I was like, "That's the trick."
When he died, there was this huge outpouring of sadness from this country and beyond. There are people who perhaps only know him from his books. Tell us a little bit more about Andrew.

It's hard to talk about Andrew without sounding hyperbolic, but he really was a lovely man. He was smart, funny and talented. I would be remiss if I didn't mention how good-looking he was. People really loved him.

items: Remembering celebrated Canadian thriller author Andrew Pyper

blocks.text: Many writers told stories of him and his generosity towards them, encouraging them to write, agreeing to come into classrooms to talk to students. The other thing that people kept saying was how he made them feel, he made them feel important. I think that stems from his curiosity. So when you were talking to Andrew, he didn't want to talk about himself, he wanted to hear about you and what was going on in your life.
This idea for this writing prize, in many ways, speaks to the generosity that he had. I'm sure he’d love this idea.
I think he'd be quite chuffed.
Tell me more about this prize and how the idea for this sparked.

Andrew played poker with a group of guys – writers, bookish-professor types – and he was no gambler, but he was dedicated to this group. About six months after Andrew died, Craig Davidson came to me and floated the idea, asked me what I thought and if it was OK if they tried to pursue this. Of course, I thought it was a wonderful idea.

Then he made the mistake of asking if I wanted to help. I'm sure he regretted that because I'd show up with my to-do list and a work-back schedule. But it came out of love and friendship amongst these men who played cards together.
But also from the fact that Andrew, despite the fact that he was a bestseller and wrote great books, didn't get the nod from some of those "literary prizes in Canada."
Yes, I think that was a frustration for him that he was disqualified before even being considered.

It wasn't like he was nominated and didn't win. It feels like there's a gap. Genre props up the publishing industry, people gobble it up. Movies and television are made from our writing, and it feels like a missing piece in the awards landscape. They recognized that, and the Pyper Prize began in that spirit.
It'll be $20,000.
It's a good chunk of change.

I think that's the distinction. There are awards for thriller writers and horror writers that exist. There's the [Bram Stoker Award], the Shirley Jackson [Award], I think there's the International Thriller Writers Awards but none of them come with a prize purse. So this really is a one-of-a-kind prize, not just in Canada, but we have yet to find one that is the equivalent.
The prize arrives at the same time as his new book comes out.

Yes. So Andrew left us with a few final words. Driven is the third and final book under his pseudonym Mason Coile. So the confluence of these two things happening at the same time is really meaningful.
How are you doing in all of this?

It's a lot, I'm not going to lie. I say it's very weird to have someone who has left us be so top of mind and such an ongoing concern, I kind of live with him in my head. I've elected to keep his social media active. His publisher offered to do it, but I just felt like I wanted to keep control of that.
In some ways, the book and the prize mean that the legacy lives on, there's a voice that’s still there.

I just reread Driven a couple of weeks ago. I read it when he finished it, but he was so sick when he was writing, it was right at the end of his life. He had said to me, "Should I write another book?" And I said, "Yeah, what else are you going to do? It's the thing that's going to get you up in the morning.” I started to read it then, but it was too dark. I said, “Our life is too scary for me to read this.” So I just read it again and you can really hear his voice. The sound of it is very clear in my mind.
Interview produced by Enza Uda

articles.title: Malaysia’s ‘alliance allergy’ and its eyes on Balabac
articles.summary: A Philippine think tank meets with counterparts in Kuala Lumpur to bridge gaps

blocks.text: A Philippine think tank meets with counterparts in Kuala Lumpur to bridge gaps

items: Malaysia is part of the Five Power Defense Arrangements and has the US as its biggest defense partner, indicating a complex security landscape.
Malaysia was the first country to protest China's nine-dash line claim and has a nuanced approach to its relations with China, balancing its economic interests with regional diplomacy.
The Philippines and Malaysia have different strategic orientations, with Malaysia being ASEAN-centric while the Philippines is more alliance-centric, affecting their responses to regional tensions.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

After three days of meetings with Malaysian think tanks, academics, and a few from the private sector in Kuala Lumpur, it dawned on me that I knew little about our neighbor. It turns out that my knowledge of this co-founder of ASEAN, an important member, is superficial.
Here are four takeaways that give me a nuanced understanding of Malaysia, a more complex country than what some of us perceive it to be — as simply pro-China.

items: Malaysia is part of the Five Power Defense Arrangements with Australia, New Zealand, United Kingdom, and Singapore. They agreed to consult each other in the event of an armed attack against Malaysia and Singapore. Every year, they hold joint military exercises.
The US is Malaysia’s biggest defense partner.
Malaysia was the first country, together with Vietnam, to protest China’s nine-dash line claim, a day after China submitted its nine-dash line map to the UN in May 2009.
Malaysia was the first ASEAN member country to open diplomatic ties with China in 1974.

blocks.text: A Philippine think tank, FACTS Asia, organized a visit to Kuala Lumpur to engage in Track Two diplomacy, an avenue where retired government officials, academics and analysts discuss issues—from the contentious to the benign—in an informal manner. The talks, governed by the Chatham House rule, were spiced up by provocative questions, straightforward and honest answers, and a sprinkling of humor.

It was my first time to participate in such a mission. It gave me a glimpse of how two sides try to understand each other’s position and suggest paths forward, a way of bridging gaps and planting seeds of ideas that may eventually reach policymakers.

Julio Amador III , FACTS Asia founder, led the delegation composed of retired Supreme Court senior associate justice Antonio Carpio, former ambassador Laura del Rosario , analyst Jesse Pascasio , Deryk Baladjay, lecturer at the De La Salle University international studies department, and myself.

A few days before we left for Kuala Lumpur, a story broke on Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim raising concern over Balabac, an island in Southern Palawan, where the US military has a rotational presence. It is close to Malaysia’s Banggi island, about 20 minutes by speedboat.

Balabac is one of the sites under EDCA, the PH-US Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement. A three-kilometer military airstrip has been reportedly constructed there, and Balikatan exercises with US and Australian forces have taken place there as well.

“As a neighboring country closely affected by claims over Sabah [Banggi Island is in Sabah], we are somewhat concerned with the tension, even though our bilateral relations with the Philippines remain very good,” Anwar was quoted as saying in a budget event in the capital Putrajaya. He said that their “basic defense capabilities must be strengthened.”

The Philippines is beefing up its defense capabilities in Balabac as part of its deterrence against China. As we know, the province of Palawan is a witness to the tension between the Philippines and China in the West Philippine Sea.

I was surprised that Anwar viewed it through a different lens. A Malaysian think tank official said this concern was coming from the “possibility of miscalculation which may rope in Malaysia” which wants to stay neutral.
The leading lights in our delegation explained the Philippine side.

I learned about Malaysia’s “allergy” to alliance from international relations professor Cheng-chwee Kuik of the Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia (National University of Malaysia). He told us they have a different “strategic DNA” from the Philippines. Malaysia considers itself ASEAN-centric and actively engages in ASEAN Plus (with dialogue partners) platforms while his country sees the Philippines as more “alliance-centric.”

Among ASEAN member countries, only two — the Philippines and Thailand — are treaty allies of the US. The alliance between Manila and Washington, DC is rooted in security cooperation and appears more robust than that of Bangkok and Washington, DC. “As US and Thai regional strategies have fallen out of alignment, trust between the two partners has waned. The United States can increase security alignment by rebuilding trust with the Royal Thai Army,” the CSIS Center for Strategic and International Studies wrote in 2021.
This makes the Philippines stand out in ASEAN. Kuik made no value judgment on the Philippines’ position; each country is distinct.

For our part, some of us perceive Malaysia as leaning towards China. As a South China Sea claimant country, it practices quiet diplomacy with China and keeps its protests against Beijing’s intrusion into its Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) under wraps — vastly different from our approach.
We shared this perception with the academics, analysts, and researchers we met. A number of them said they are concerned about China’s activities but are not alarmed.
Malaysia has been successful in one area where we have failed, so far.

Petronas, the state-owned oil and gas company, has drilled for gas in Kasawari field, a major offshore natural gas development in the South China Sea, off the coast of Sarawak and within their EEZ, but which China claims.

Petronas has been no stranger to China Coast Guard vessels that have intruded into their EEZ. But it is common for Malaysia’s Navy and Maritime Enforcement Agency to keep watch and shadow the Chinese vessels.
After all, this is a matter of economic survival for Malaysia, the second-highest producer of petroleum in Southeast Asia and the fifth-highest exporter of liquefied natural gas (LNG) globally.
Let me know what you think. You can email me at marites.vitug@rappler.com.
Till next newsletter!

articles.title: Nepal says big polluters must ‘wake up’ as it calls for climate compensation over flood disaster
articles.summary:
Foreign minister Shisir Khanal tells the Guardian the world’s biggest economies need to help Nepal, which contributes less than 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions

Nepal is demanding…

blocks.text: Nepal is demanding $20m in climate compensation for the recent devastating floods, as a senior minister called on the world’s most polluting countries to “wake up” and accept shared responsibility for a disaster that led to the death or disappearance of more than 6,000 people.

Scientists believe the climate crisis had a role to play in the floods, which were triggered when a melting glacier partially collapsed and set off a deadly landslide and flash flooding through Chinese-controlled Tibet and Nepal in late August. So far, more than 1,300 are confirmed dead and more than 5,500 still missing, with hopes of their survival diminished after 12 days of rescue operations.

Speaking to the Guardian, Nepal’s foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, was forthright in his call for climate justice and said it was imperative the world’s biggest economies stepped up to help Nepal recover and rebuild after the catastrophic floods.

Nepal contributes less than 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions, while its neighbours India and China are among the world’s biggest emitters. The mountains of the Himalayas – which span across India, China, Nepal and Bhutan – have been warming at a rate nearly 50% faster than the global average.
In 2023, the UN said Nepal’s mountains had lost close to a third of their ice in just over 30 years due to global heating.

Khanal emphasised that the recent disaster was far more extreme than any flooding regularly seen during the monsoon season, and said the magnitude of damage was on par with the 2015 earthquake that left much of the country in ruins.

blocks.caption: An excavator repairs a damaged road in Nepal near the Trishuli River on Monday. Photograph: Anushree Fadnavis/Reuters

blocks.text: “This felt like a tsunami that was coming from the Himalayas,” he said. “We experienced waves as high as 60, 70 feet, which were mixed with debris, mud, stones, rocks, and came at the speed of almost 180km per hour. Towns, villages and highways were completely wiped out and there are some areas still disconnected.”

Khanal confirmed that Nepal’s ministry of finance and ministry of environment had written a joint letter to the UN’s fund for responding to loss and damage – which was set up in 2022 in line with the Paris climate agreement – to request $20m in climate-related damages.

“We have contributed so little to climate change,” he said. “It is imperative for those in the global community who benefit from larger, much more polluting economies, and whose historical contribution to greenhouse gases is much bigger than ours, to accept a shared responsibility. This affects all of humanity.”
For Nepal, the disaster was particularly worrying because it was “one of the strongest warning signals that we’ve experienced of what’s to come”, he said.

“The global community should not see this as one-off disaster; it should be viewed in the context of the changing climate in the Himalayas,” he said. “We know it is going to be a recurring scenario that more and more communities, not just in Nepal but around the world, will have to face.”

Khanal acknowledged that the compensation amount Nepal has requested from the UN was “obviously not nearly enough to cover the damage that we have sustained”. According to some estimates, the total damage caused by the floods will be upwards of $5bn, though Khanal said it could be even higher.

Upwards of 20,000 homes will probably have to be rebuilt, as well as the main highway. Villages built in vulnerable areas along the river, some of which washed away entirely, may have to be relocated to higher, safer ground.

While Khanal initially singled out India and China as countries that should step in to help – while avoiding mention of the US, which is the world’s biggest polluter – he rowed back on those comments, saying: “It is not just about shifting the blame to one or the other country, it’s about us all working together.”

blocks.caption: Damaged buildings on the banks of the Trishuli River. Photograph: Anushree Fadnavis/Reuters

blocks.text: He emphasised that the compensation demand was also meant to act as a “wake-up call for the global community to establish a more robust mechanism to help vulnerable and small economies like Nepal”.

The UN has admitted the loss and damage fund is already facing a “significant financing gap”. The fund has already received requests totalling $2.8bn from about 119 countries, but so far only around $400m has been given by the international community. The US has given just $17m, after Donald Trump withdrew from the Paris agreement.
Khanal acknowledged there were “political challenges” in getting Nepal the climate compensation it was demanding.
“Yes there always will be people who may not agree to our perspective or deny there is climate change, but there are also people who deny that the Earth is round,” he said bluntly.
He emphasised the importance of funds being made available not just for immediate disaster response but also for preparedness and mitigation for climate-related risk.

Khanal rebuffed allegations that China had failed to give an adequate warning or share data with Nepal about the impending floods. He said he was in discussion with China about enhancing coordination and data sharing for the Himalayan region.
“With the benefit of hindsight, we can now see that this glacier was fragile and had been receding in the past six months,” he said.

“But before the floods hit, there was no knowledge on our part, or on the part of Chinese scientists, that this particular collapse was imminent. I do not believe any of us had any idea of the threat until it happened.”

articles.title: [Ask the Tax Whiz] Should billionaires pay more?
articles.summary: A wealth tax without modern tax administration risks becoming a classic Philippine reform: good policy on paper, weak enforcement in practice.

items: The proposal for a wealth tax in the Philippines aims to impose annual rates on net taxable assets above certain thresholds, but effective tax administration is crucial for its success.
Current revenue collection heavily relies on voluntary compliance, highlighting the need for a modern tax administration that can accurately identify and verify wealth.
Before implementing a wealth tax, the government must distinguish between legitimate and ill-gotten wealth, ensuring that tax policies do not hinder productive investment.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
Should billionaires pay more?

Yes. But before Congress creates another tax, government must answer a more basic question: Can it identify the real billionaires, determine what they actually own, and verify whether that wealth was legitimately earned and properly taxed?

House Bill No. 9274 proposes annual rates of 1% on net taxable assets above ₱1 billion, 2% above ₱2 billion, and 3% above ₱3 billion. Greater progressivity is a defensible objective. But a wealth tax without modern tax administration risks becoming a classic Philippine reform: good policy on paper, weak enforcement in practice.
The most revealing number is not the proposed 3% rate.

According to the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR)’s 2025 Annual Report, ₱3.03 trillion—or 97.55% of total collections—came from voluntary payments. Preliminary and final assessments contributed only 2.33%, while delinquent accounts added 0.12%.

That does not make audit unimportant. Tax audit and investigation deter tax evasion and protect compliant taxpayers. But it tells policymakers where sustainable revenue really comes from: voluntary compliance supported by credible enforcement.

The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) similarly reports that additional assessments from audit averaged about 3% of collections among reporting tax administrations in 2023. Modern tax administrations do not finance government by auditing everyone. They use information, risk management, and targeted enforcement to encourage everyone else to comply voluntarily.
Modern tax administration should therefore be the reform—not simply another tax.

The Philippines can learn from countries that have retained wealth taxes. Switzerland integrates wealth taxation with annual income-tax reporting and established asset-valuation systems. Norway imposes combined wealth-tax rates around 1% at higher levels and provides valuation discounts for shares and operating assets. Colombia, a more relevant emerging-market example, made its wealth tax permanent, with rates from 0.5% to 1.5%.
The lesson is not that we should copy them.
Wealth taxes work best when government can see, value and verify wealth.
That is precisely where our institutional reform must begin.

The Philippines needs a modern revenue administration that is fiscally autonomous, professionally managed and politically insulated, with strong internal controls and accountability. It should integrate tax returns, beneficial ownership, property, securities, major asset acquisitions and legally accessible financial information to build verified asset-and-income profiles of high-net-worth taxpayers.
Forbes is useful for headlines. It is not a tax database.

Bank secrecy must also evolve. It should protect legitimate privacy—not unexplained wealth, tax evasion, money laundering or corruption. Reform must come with strict access rules, digital audit trails, confidentiality safeguards, and severe penalties for abuse. (READ: [Puso at Diwa] Foreign currency deposit secrecy: Time for a constitutional rethink)

Objective risk-based scrutiny should follow the evidence wherever it leads—including to public officials, politically exposed persons, political families, major campaign donors, and government contractors when declared lawful income is materially inconsistent with accumulated assets.
That is not political persecution. The best protection against weaponized taxation is an independent institution applying transparent rules and due process regardless of who is in power.

Our decades-long struggle to recover ill-gotten wealth should have taught us another lesson: once assets disappear behind nominees, corporations and layered transactions, recovery becomes far more difficult.
Government should detect unexplained wealth early—not decades later.
But tax policy must distinguish legitimate wealth from ill-gotten wealth.

An entrepreneur who builds a multibillion-peso company, creates thousands of jobs, attracts investment and pays the correct taxes is not the problem. Developing economies need successful businesses, deeper capital markets, and more investment.
Tax policy should distribute the fiscal burden more fairly—not destroy the productive wealth that creates jobs.

That is why Congress should carefully model a recurring tax as high as 3% of net wealth. Start with a genuinely ultra-high threshold. Consider moderate marginal rates. Provide tightly designed rules for productive but illiquid assets. Close artificial-debt and beneficial-ownership loopholes. Then measure actual collections, investment effects and administrative costs.

The World Bank likewise emphasizes transparency, beneficial-ownership information, international information exchange, and advanced data analytics as foundations of stronger domestic revenue mobilization, especially in developing economies.
So, should billionaires pay more?
Yes. But first build a government capable of finding the real billionaires—and distinguishing wealth created through enterprise from wealth accumulated through corruption or tax evasion.
Collect better before taxing more.
Tax verified wealth, not headlines. Modernize tax administration. Protect legitimate investment. Follow unexplained wealth wherever it leads.
Otherwise, we may create another tax that looks progressive on paper—while the truly rich and powerful remain beyond its reach. – Rappler.com

Mon Abrea, CPA, MBA, MPA (Harvard) is a global tax policy expert and Chief Tax Advisor of Asian Consulting Group (ACGlobal). He advises governments, multinational enterprises, and international organizations on tax policy, investment competitiveness, and fiscal reform. He is the author of Reimagining the World Without Corruption and Why Invest in the Philippines? CREATE MORE Edition, and has represented the Philippines in policy dialogues at the OECD, World Bank, and other international forums.

articles.title: Iran warns US energy assets in Gulf are vulnerable after latest clashes
articles.summary: The ongoing conflict is severely impacting Iran's economy and oil exports, while also affecting Gulf Arab states and contributing to rising fuel prices in the US

blocks.text: A statue symbolising the hand of Iran's late Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei next to a billboard depicting US President Donald Trump laid in a coffin, in Tehran, Iran, on July 23, 2026.
via REUTERS
The ongoing conflict is severely impacting Iran's economy and oil exports, while also affecting Gulf Arab states and contributing to rising fuel prices in the US

items: Iran has threatened retaliation against US attacks on its assets, warning that energy infrastructure in the Gulf is vulnerable.
Tensions have escalated with recent strikes between the US and Iran, and Iran has announced new restrictions on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

DUBAI, UAE – Iran threatened on Monday, September 7, to retaliate against any new US attacks on its assets, warning that energy infrastructure across the Gulf, including US oil and gas interests, was vulnerable.

“Strike our assets and you get struck,” Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf said after US and Iranian strikes on shipping at the weekend that pushed oil prices up near six-week highs on Monday.

The latest threat underscores the risks of further escalation after the sides traded blows again at the weekend, with no sign of progress towards a diplomatic breakthrough that could end more than six months of conflict and restore normal energy flows through the Gulf.
Iran has tightened restrictions on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical artery for global oil and gas supplies, since the war began with US and Israeli strikes on February 28.
On Sunday, September 6, senior Iranian security official Mohsen Rezaei said Tehran would soon announce a new restricted zone in the Gulf and unveil a new shipping corridor through the strait.
Rezaei said the zone would begin where a US naval blockade of Iran starts and extend into parts of the Gulf.
Any vessel entering the area would be placed on an Iranian sanctions list.
“We will only commit to the Strait of Hormuz being open when they (the Americans) stop the sabotage, threats and attacks on Iran,” Rezaei said.
Qalibaf later reinforced Tehran’s warning in what appeared to be a response to US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who had described Iran’s oil tanker fleet as “defenseless.”

“It’s simple: the oil and gas production chain here is sprawling, accessible, and exposed. American oil and gas companies across these waters and facilities share that exposure,” Qalibaf, who is Iran’s top negotiator, wrote on X.

Regional tensions were heightened by Israeli strikes on a town in southern Lebanon that killed at least 12 people on Monday, according to Lebanon’s health ministry, marking one of the deadliest days of bombardment in recent weeks.

The attacks have fueled fears of a renewed Israeli military campaign despite a June ceasefire with the Iran-backed Hezbollah group. They also complicate efforts to end the wider conflict, with Tehran insisting that any lasting agreement with Washington must include an end to Israeli attacks in Lebanon.

US President Donald Trump has yet to achieve the aims he set out when he launched “Operation Epic Fury” in February: to end Iran’s nuclear program, halt its ability to attack its neighbors and create conditions for Iranians to topple their leadership.

Tehran’s clerical rulers remain in power and aim to emerge from the war stronger than before. They continue to demand sanctions relief and hope eventually to collect fees from ships using the strait, which carried a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments before the war.
After a relative lull through much of August, hostilities have intensified again following the collapse of an interim ceasefire reached in June. Diplomatic efforts have made little headway.

On Saturday, September 5, US forces struck three Iranian oil tankers, including one near Kharg Island, Iran’s main oil export hub, according to US Central Command. The attacks followed strikes by Iran’s Revolutionary Guards on US warships operating in the region.
Tehran has demonstrated it can still attack US interests in neighboring countries and disrupt oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz.
Shipping data showed an average of just 10 commodity vessels per day transited the strait over the past 10 days, the lowest level since May.
Iran has said it will step up efforts to tackle problems created by US sanctions that are crippling its economy.

Yet the pressure is mounting. Three senior Iranian sources told Reuters that Washington’s campaign to choke off Iranian oil exports and curb sanctions evasion is becoming increasingly difficult for Tehran to withstand.

Qalibaf acknowledged at the weekend that Iran’s struggle was no longer confined to the battlefield. Alongside the military confrontation, he said, the country faced major domestic challenges including inflation, unemployment, currency volatility and market instability.

The conflict has also impacted oil-producing Gulf Arab states such as the United Arab Emirates, which has come under fire from Iranian missiles and suffered attacks on its oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz.
UAE presidential adviser Anwar Gargash said on Monday the country was building alternative routes for its energy exports and trade to ensure they are not “held hostage” by the war.

The disruption has also been felt in the United States, where higher fuel prices have added to economic pressures and weighed on Trump’s popularity ahead of November’s midterm elections that will determine control of Congress. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Rescued endangered hawk-eagle eaglet turned over to DENR in Zamboanga
articles.summary: PAGADIAN CITY, Zamboanga del Sur – A juvenile South Philippine Hawk-Eagle (Nisaetus pinskeri), an endangered raptor endemic to the country, was rescued and turned over to environmental authorities…

blocks.text: PAGADIAN CITY, Zamboanga del Sur – A juvenile South Philippine Hawk-Eagle (Nisaetus pinskeri), an endangered raptor endemic to the country, was rescued and turned over to environmental authorities Sunday, September 6, offering a rare sign of hope for the survival of the threatened species.

The young bird was retrieved at Barangay Sas in Gutalac town, Zamboanga del Norte by a team from the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) Community Environment and Natural Resources Office (CENRO) Liloy.

Initial physical assessments revealed the eaglet is in good condition despite months away from its natural habitat. The juvenile raptor is currently housed at the CENRO Liloy Wildlife Holding Facility, where wildlife officers are conducting further evaluation and health monitoring to prepare the bird for eventual release back into the wild.

The bird’s journey to safety began three months ago when Justine Jay Sapalleda and his friends heard distress calls coming from a fallen nest in a nearby tree. Finding the crying eaglet vulnerable and abandoned, the children brought it home to protect it.

For three months, the Sapalleda family sheltered and fed the juvenile eagle a diet of fish and chicken meat. Unaware that keeping protected wildlife is illegal under Philippine law, the family raised the bird through its most delicate developmental stage before local resident Jessica Pagente learned of the situation and alerted CENRO Liloy.

“The timely report and the care extended by the Sapalleda family helped ensure the juvenile eagle’s safety and provided it with an opportunity to return to the wild,” CENRO Liloy chief Maribel Acama said, highlighting the vital role local communities play in conservation efforts.
Also known as Pinsker’s hawk-eagle, the species is classified as “endangered” under DENR Administrative Order No. 2019-09 due to severe habitat loss and poaching.

Following the turnover, CENRO Liloy reminded the public that holding or keeping wildlife is prohibited, urging citizens to immediately report displaced, injured, or threatened animals to the nearest DENR office for proper rescue and rehabilitation. INQ

articles.title: Second-hand smoke causes to nearly 1.7M deaths globally – study
articles.summary: PARIS — More than 2.7 billion people including children have been exposed to second-hand smoke globally, contributing to nearly 1.7 million deaths in 2023, according to study published Tuesday…

blocks.text: PARIS — More than 2.7 billion people including children have been exposed to second-hand smoke globally, contributing to nearly 1.7 million deaths in 2023, according to study published Tuesday in The Lancet.

Tobacco remains a leading cause of disease globally, the study said, noting many “non-smokers exposed to second-hand smoke” were among the estimate total of 8 million people who died in 2023 of smoking-related illnesses.
“Exposure to second-hand smoke is a globally recognized health risk, with no safe level of inhalation,” it said.

By reviewing studies published in the US National Institutes of Health database PubMed along with population surveys, Tuesday’s study sought to estimate the prevalence of exposure to second-hand smoke and quantify the burden of disease in 204 countries and territories between 1990 and 2023.
Among the approximately 2.7 billion people exposed to second-hand smoke in 2023 were 767 million children aged 0 to 14, the study found.

This exposure is estimated to have resulted in 1.66 million premature deaths and causing premature disability and illness, leading with ischemic heart disease, a heart condition caused by insufficient oxygen supply to the heart muscle.
In children, exposure to second-hand smoke is estimated to have caused 5.2 million respiratory tract infections in 2023, it said.
People in proximity to someone lighting up are exposed to both the “sidestream smoke” from the burning tobacco product and smoke exhaled by the active smoker, the study explained.

“The sidestream component, which dominates the air non-smokers breathe, is unfiltered… carrying higher per-unit concentrations of the toxic and carcinogenic compounds” than that being inhaled by the active smoker, it said.

Despite significant declines in smoking prevalence globally since 1990, the absolute number of people exposed has remained stable due to population growth and increased exposure in Africa and the Middle East.
Women are also disproportionately affected by second-hand smoke, particularly in regions where smoking prevalence among women is low, it noted.
“Despite this substantial burden, (second-hand smoke) exposure remains rarely acknowledged as a major risk factor for female health,” it said.
The study called for governments to implement stronger tobacco controls in public places and in homes in order to better protect women and children from second-hand smoke. /dl

articles.title: Medicine shortages, missed targets delay tuberculosis healthcare delivery
articles.summary: Bid notices for TB medicine show two failed and four canceled biddings from 2023 to 2025, resulting in shortages

blocks.text: Second of two partsPart 1 | IN NUMBERS: Decades of tuberculosis in the Philippines
Despite being highly curable, tuberculosis (TB) has persisted in the Philippines for over two decades, with the country ranking third globally in terms of TB burden in 2024.
As case counts continue to climb, experts point to medicine procurement failures in 2023-2024 that caused supply shortages and disrupted treatment for about 700,000 people with TB.
Bid notices for TB medicine under the main office of the Department of Health (DOH) showed two failed and four canceled biddings from 2023 to 2025.

The first failed bid, in October 2023, targeted medicine worth P966 million. It was rescheduled to January 2024, but was canceled. The office issued another P966-million bid in August 2024, which also failed.

The order for pediatrics medicine for TB and bedaquiline, a medicine for drug-resistant TB (DR-TB) patients — with approved budgets of P117 million and P112 million, respectively — did not push through at all, according to the Philippine Government Electronic Procurement System (PhilGEPS).
PhilGEPS is a centralized platform for government agencies to post public bidding opportunities, award notices, and procurement activities for registered suppliers.

No bidding happened because of either a failure of bids or a cancellation altogether. According to documents cited by PhilGEPS, a failure of bids is declared when there are no bid submissions, the prospective bidders are ineligible, they did not comply with the bid requirements, or there was no award of contract.
Meanwhile, an agency’s Bids and Awards Committee can cancel a bid if the project becomes unfeasible or unnecessary, if funding is cut or withheld, or if a calamity or quarantine is declared.
In the case of the TB medicines, no specific reasons were cited for the bid failures or the cancellations.
All failed and canceled procurements, despite rebiddings, cost over P2 billion.
Dr. Jan Llevado, DOH Disease Control and Prevention Bureau director, pointed out that suppliers find it challenging to procure the DOH’s bulk orders as they mostly rely on manufacturers’ supplies.
“So the question is how the DOH can do a more reliable [multi-year] forecast so that the industry is also informed,” Llevado said in a mix of English and Filipino.
She also confirmed that there are drug-susceptible TB (DS-TB) medicine shortages across multiple regions, raising the risk factor for increasing drug-resistant TB (DR-TB) cases.

Drug-susceptible TB treatment requires consistent, six-month medication regimens of two to four drugs. Those with drug resistance may require up to 18 months, depending on their condition, with more medicines to take.
Straying from the regimen for just a few days could complicate the disease. Those with drug-susceptible TB could potentially develop drug resistance, too.

While the treatment is free in government-run health facilities, patients facing low supply may resort to buying their own. A six-month regimen for a DS-TB patient could cost more than P2,000, while a DR-TB patient may spend up to P400,000.

The TB Health Education and Livelihood Support Community, Inc. (TB HEALS), a non-profit organization, said that they received 30 reports of medicine shortages or stockouts in various regions from 2025 to August 2026.

blocks.caption: visualization

blocks.text: Their data comes from TB HEALS’ KomuKonek, a community feedback platform for reporting local health center TB service concerns.
Their data currently show 20 DS-TB medicine stockout cases for the four-drug fixed-dose combinations (FDC), followed by the two-drug regimen.
Four in total complained of DR-TB drug stockouts, while one said they’re short on TB preventive treatment (TPT).
Eight complaints came from Western Visayas, then seven from Calabarzon.
Florita Dalida, TB HEALS president, stressed that shortages threaten not just the patient, but also the people around them.
“For a disease like TB, shouldn’t it be treated as an emergency? Because if you don’t get treated, you can infect up to 15 people within a year,” Dalida said.
Besides shortages, experts also monitor how the Philippines, through its national TB control program, accomplishes yearly targets.

Following the first phase’s unmet goals during the pandemic, the DOH is implementing its Philippine Strategic TB Elimination Plan Phase 2, or PhilSTEP 2 (2025–2030), to address the nation’s enduring TB crisis.
PhilSTEP 2 is a roadmap that envisions reducing the country’s TB mortality rate, incidence rate, and catastrophic costs by 2030, by following set objectives.

blocks.caption: Page, Text, File

blocks.text: The four objectives follow the cascade of care framework for TB — screening, testing, treatment, and prevention.

items: A presumptive patient is screened via chest X-ray (CXR) or artificial intelligence computer-aided detection (CAD) software for signs of TB.
If positive, they will be tested further and diagnosed. This process determines whether the patient has DS-TB, which responds to first-line medication, or DR-TB.
The confirmed TB patient is registered in the system and placed under Directly Observed Treatment, Short-course, or DOTS. Healthcare providers will determine which drugs to take and how much.
To prevent transmission, contact tracing is conducted. Those with higher risk, asymptomatic patients, or people exposed to active cases are given preventive treatment.

blocks.text: How is the Philippines faring in achieving these goals?
This graph shows a comparison of regional performance on presumptive tuberculosis testing targets for 2025 and the first and second quarters of 2026. Hover over each region for more details.
Although the country reached a national screening rate of 98% in 2025, regional progress remains uneven.

BARMM has the lowest rate at 8%, with Bicol coming up next at 15%. Six regions have not reached the 50-percent mark. Another six regions have reached more than a 100% screening rate, pulling up the national average.
The DOH, along with the World Health Organization (WHO), has set a target of 12 million Filipinos screened for TB by 2026, as part of the commitment to prevent the disease.
As of August 2026, the screening rate has reached only a quarter of the annual target, with the same regions lagging as last year.
Even then, not everyone screened for TB underwent testing. The annual presumptive testing target for 2025 of 1.8 million people was 75% accomplished. Testing for 2026 is at 26% as of August.
Llevado noted that cartridge procurement issues for GenExpert machines — used to diagnose TB and detect drug resistance — drove down 2026 testing rates compared to the same period in 2025.
Based on notification rates, the DOH recorded the following treatment success rates for new and relapse DS-TB and DR-TB cases.

blocks.caption: visualization

blocks.text: Drug-susceptible TB treatment had an average success rate of 91.3% from 2018 to 2025, while drug-resistant TB stood at 70.8%.
The success rate for the latter dropped by 10% from 2024 to 2025, which mirrors the gaps the WHO mentioned in treating drug-resistant and multidrug-resistant cases.

The Philippines also has gaps in preventive treatment, which Llevado considers a low-hanging fruit. As an airborne disease, it is important to treat TB before it even becomes an active case to prevent transmission, she stressed.

She added that for the DOH, strengthening programs is crucial. “We should find TB earlier, we should test accurately, we should initiate treatment immediately,” Llevado said, adding that the DOH should ensure the continuity and completion of treatment.
The health department is currently evaluating bids from September 3 to 10 and promised that TB medicine supplies will be delivered by October or November this year. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Eiffel Tower shut by staff protest after women moved for religious visit
articles.summary: The mayor of Paris said an investigation would be launched into the incident, which left female employees "humiliated", according to a union representative.

blocks.text: The Eiffel Tower was closed on Monday after staff went on strike over female workers being removed for the visit of a Hindu religious group, workers and management said.
A delegation of around 100 people linked to the Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) group visited the landmark in the French capital on Saturday.
Staff union representative Diane Davoine says as they arrived at the monument, women were told to move.

"During the visit of this delegation, women were asked to leave their places of work in order to place men there," she told Reuters. Davoine also said management had since apologised to workers over the incident.
"So that absolutely does not go down well with the employees, with women obviously, who are all humiliated by what happened, by the way some were treated," Davoine said.

She added: "Tensions mounted over the weekend, so this morning, the employees decided to meet: first, to open a dialogue with management, and second, to ensure that women are never treated this way at the company again."

Société d'Exploitation de la tour Eiffel (SETE), the company that operates the monument in Paris, confirmed the delegation had asked the visit be organised to limit "interactions with women", according to the AFP news agency.
The firm told AFP that "these conditions should not have been accepted".
They added they "were not in line with SETE's values, nor with the principles of equality between men and women".
SETE president Ariel Weil said: "It is clearly not an acceptable practice.
"I restate the Eiffel Tower's commitment to republican values and to the equality of men and women."
The BBC has contacted the Union Confédération générale du travail (CGT) for a response.
BAPS consecrated its first major temple in France on Sunday, in the suburbs of Paris.

In a statement on X, the BAPS temple in Paris said their trip was "arranged in conjunction with the Eiffel Tower team at the start of normal opening hours to avoid disrupting or inconveniencing others".
It apologised "for any pain or inconvenience caused", adding "we believe in the universal values of mutual respect and service".
On its website, BAPS describes itself as a "spiritual, volunteer-driven fellowship dedicated to improving society" through Hindu values.
It has temples in major cities around the world, including London, Los Angeles and Sydney.
Paris Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire said there would be an investigation into the circumstances of the visit.
"I am taking note of the anger expressed by the employees of the Eiffel Tower, and I want to tell them that their discontent is legitimate," he wrote on X.
"Equality between women and men will never stop at the foot of our historical monuments, nor anywhere in this city. It must be applied everywhere, for everyone."
French hard-right leader Marine Le Pen said: "In France, we will never accept that the presence of women be 'limited'."

Former centre-right French Prime Minister Gabriel Attal, who has said he will run for the presidency next year, said: "In France, no culture, no belief, no worship, nothing nor anyone can come to dictate to women their place."
Yaël Braun-Pivet, the president of France's National Assembly, said: "I refuse to allow women to be compelled to step aside in order to meet the demands of foreign visitors."

articles.title: Highlights: Day 22 of Sara Duterte impeachment trial | Sept. 7, 2026
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – The 22nd day of Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial focused on the identities of alleged recipients of confidential funds released by the Office of the Vice…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – The 22nd day of Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial focused on the identities of alleged recipients of confidential funds released by the Office of the Vice President (OVP) and the Department of Education (DepEd).

Philippine Statistics Authority Assistant National Statistician Marizza Grande testified for the prosecution and confirmed that several names listed as confidential fund payees could not be found in the agency’s civil registry records.

Grande’s testimony covered the unusual or unique names of individuals who signed acknowledgment receipts used by the Office of the Vice President and the Department of Education to liquidate their P612.5 million in confidential funds.

In a notable development, defense counsel Justin Gular, responding to a query from Senator-judge Risa Hontiveros, acknowledged for the first time during the proceedings that the names on the acknowledgment receipts are aliases.
Senator-judge Raffy Tulfo said the use of aliases could be forgivable, but described the similar signatures and handwriting on the receipts as very questionable.

Presiding officer Sen. Francis Escudero separately announced that the impeachment court may summon witnesses on its own should it see the need to, after Senator-judge Erwin Tulfo expressed hope that former VPSPG officials Col. Dennis Nolasco and Col. Raymund Lachica would be called despite the prosecution indicating it no longer needed them.

Meanwhile, Senator Robin Padilla, a self-described ally of the Duterte family, argued in a manifestation that the immunity from suit enjoyed by the president should be extended to the vice president, citing the constitutional purpose of protecting impeachable officers from harassment and distraction.
Outside the impeachment court, Malacañang assured Sara Duterte the PNP would not be used as a weapon against her, after she posted bail Saturday on three grave threats counts./dp

articles.title: US woman charged with killing son ‘very invested’ in Lindsay Clancy trial, prosecutors say
articles.summary:
Corie Walsh charged with murder after two-year-old Barrett found dead in basement of Illinois family home last week

An Illinois woman charged with killing her two-year-old son had been…

blocks.text: An Illinois woman charged with killing her two-year-old son had been closely following the murder trial of Massachusetts mother Lindsay Clancy and was texting friends about the case just hours before her son was found dead, prosecutors said.

Corie Walsh, 40, was charged with three counts of first-degree murder after her son, Barrett, was found dead in the basement of the family’s suburban Chicago home last Tuesday, according to court records obtained by NBC Chicago.

Prosecutors said Walsh had become “very invested” in Clancy’s nationally watched trial and was discussing it with friends until about 12:30pm. that day. A neighbor found Barrett less than four hours later.

Walsh was found elsewhere in the home with injuries authorities said were self-inflicted. Prosecutors said she later told investigators that she killed her son because she believed he was the “devil” and the “anti-Christ”. Her attorney, Andrea Lyon, told reporters Walsh was experiencing a psychotic episode and called the boy’s death a tragedy for the entire family.

Police were called to Walsh’s home in Frankfort, about 35 miles south-west of Chicago, shortly before 4pm after a neighbor discovered Barrett in the basement, according to prosecutors’ petition seeking to keep Walsh jailed before trial.

The neighbor found the boy and began CPR while calling 911, prosecutors said. He was taken to a hospital, where he was pronounced dead. An autopsy determined that he died from asphyxia caused by ligature compression of the neck.

Police searching the house found Walsh fully dressed in a bathtub containing bloody water, prosecutors said. She had cuts to her wrists and thighs and was taken to a hospital with injuries authorities described as not life-threatening.
The disclosure that Walsh had been following Clancy’s trial came days after a Massachusetts judge declared a mistrial in that case when jurors said they could not reach a unanimous verdict.

Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse, was accused of killing her three young children in 2023. Her lawyers argued that she was legally insane and suffering from postpartum psychosis. Prosecutors maintained that Clancy understood what she was doing and knew it was wrong.

Authorities in Illinois have not alleged that Clancy’s trial played a role in the killing of Walsh’s son, and no evidence made public so far establishes a connection beyond her discussion of the case.
Frankfort police and prosecutors in Will county did not respond to calls for comment on Monday.

articles.title: A food safety officer has become a social media star in India - why?
articles.summary: Tukaram Mundhe has gone viral after a series of aggressive inspections of restaurants to detect hygiene lapses.

blocks.text: The images are hard to ignore.
Cockroaches scurry across kitchen floors. Spider webs cling to walls. Spoiled vegetables rot in corners, while food counters show signs of pest infestation.
One might assume these scenes belong to a struggling restaurant. But the photos are from a members-only club in Mumbai - India's financial capital and the capital of its richest state Maharashtra.

They are among dozens of photos and videos that have gone viral since May, after Maharashtra's Food and Drug Administration (FDA) began a series of inspections at restaurants, cafes and other food businesses across the state.
At the centre of the crackdown is 51-year-old civil servant Tukaram Mundhe, the state's new food commissioner.
Since taking charge in May, Mundhe has overseen thousands of inspections and says food safety laws must be enforced regardless of a business's size, influence or reputation.

His department has suspended the licences of several quick-commerce warehouses and sent notices to Bollywood celebrities for doing advertisements suspected of indirectly promoting restricted products.
"These actions are taken in public health interest. We will continue to take them against violations," Mundhe told the BBC.
The campaign has made Mundhe a recognisable face across India, rare for a civil servant.
Videos of his inspections and press briefings circulate widely on social media, where reels and podcasts have turned him into an unlikely celebrity.
But the spotlight - and the controversy that often comes with it - is nothing new to him.

An officer in the Indian Administrative Service, Mundhe has more than two decades of experience and has been transferred so often that reports say the number exceeds his years in service, though he declines to confirm it.
"I have stopped counting my transfers," he told the BBC.
Admirers see the transfers as evidence of his uncompromising style. Critics argue that this confrontational approach has put him at odds with colleagues and elected representatives.

In the past decade, Mundhe has won praise for his handling of the Covid pandemic outbreak during his time as Nagpur city's municipal commissioner and earlier for his work on water conservation in Maharashtra's drought-prone regions.

"When he was transferred out of Nagpur during the pandemic, thousands showed up outside his home to bid him farewell. It took him an hour just to reach his car," says Shafi Pathan, a journalist who's written Mundhe's biography in the local Marathi language.
But his food-safety crackdown has brought him the most attention yet.
The scale of India's food-safety problem is serious and numbers presented to the parliament in July offer a glimpse of just how widespread the issue is.
Of 223,808 food samples tested across India in 2025 and 2026, nearly one in five, external were found to be "non-conforming" - which means the samples were either unsafe, substandard or mislabelled.
And Mundhe has responded with an unusually aggressive enforcement drive.
By the end of July, his department had carried out more than 3,100 inspections across the state - a number he expects has since crossed 4,000.
Around 300 licences had been suspended and more than 1,000 improvement notices issued. A new complaints portal had also received more than 16,000 complaints in its first three months, Mundhe said.
"Hygiene has always been a problem here," Pawan Agarwal, former chief of India's food regulator, told the BBC. "What Mundhe has done differently is make it visible".

Consumers have responded positively to that visibility, Agarwal says. Unlike in India's conventional system, where food safety cases and consumer complaints can take years to move through regulators and courts, enforcement actions are now playing out in public.
The campaign has also made Mundhe a social media star - he now has more than 3.8 million followers on Instagram.
However, even as consumers welcome the speed and visibility of his actions, many in the food industry are less enthusiastic.
Restaurant associations allege the official has been bypassing a statutory process, while courts have termed some of his actions "high-handed".

Under India's food safety laws, businesses are usually given time to fix violations before regulators suspend or cancel their licences. Regulators can suspend licences immediately only in urgent public health situations but must record their reasons.

"While compliance is non-negotiable, high-handed approaches - like public naming-and-shaming, instant suspensions over minor procedural or rectifiable issues and treating administrative oversights with harsh penal measures - create panic rather than reform," said Niranjan Laxman Shetty, legal chairman of hospitality association Indian Hotel and Restaurant Association.

Responding to the criticism, Mundhe said his raids are lawful and that suspensions are only for extreme cases. However, some businesses have publicly claimed that they've been shut over minor violations, without warning or a chance to improve first.
His actions have also faced legal challenges. In some cases, courts have overturned licence suspensions, ordered compensation for affected businesses and criticised the regulator's approach.

In August, for instance, the Bombay high court ordered, external Mundhe's department to pay 500,000 rupees ($5,291; £3,893) in compensation to a sweets shop whose licence remained suspended even after a reinspection found it 98% compliant with the law.
The court said the regulator's intentions were "laudable" but that it had "gone overboard".
The judges also raised a question - was the regulator applying the same scrutiny to government establishments as it was to private businesses?
Within a day of that criticism, Mundhe's team inspected canteens in the state's high court complex and flagged violations.
For Mundhe, it is proof that the rules apply equally to everyone.
"Had the food business operators or establishment complied with existing regulations, I would not be needed to take those actions," Mundhe told the BBC.
He also insists that they are not trying to shut down businesses but only ensure safety.

"We are not here to close down or suspend every licensee," he said at an event last week. "We are here to ensure food is safe, food is not substandard, it is not misbranded and it is good for consumption."
The restaurant inspections - which dominate social media - are only a part of his work.
Mundhe has enforced bans on using newspapers to wrap food, synthetic dyes and banned analogue paneer - non-dairy cottage cheese substitutes.

Its focus has now shifted to schools. The department has ordered canteens, hostel kitchens and midday meal suppliers to obtain proper licences, and banned the sale of food high in fat, sugar or salt within 50m of schools.
But the bigger question is what happens once Mundhe moves on to his next post.
"The efforts of Mundhe have created a nationwide awareness about food safety, both amongst businesses and consumers, which is desirable - but not sustainable," says Agarwal.
The challenge is to build systems that outlast an individual officer, he adds.
For now, however, the effects are being felt even on the streets.

Yuvraj Yadav, who sells sandwiches in a Mumbai suburb, says he used to wrap them in discarded newspapers, despite concerns that chemicals in the printing ink can leach into food. He recently switched to greaseproof paper after hearing about the ban.
"We started this a few months ago after newspapers were not allowed for packing as it's bad for health," he says.

articles.title: Sara Duterte trial Day 23: Reserved witness to testify on SC receipts
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The prosecution panel on Tuesday is set to present its first reserved witness to testify in Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial. Police Maj. Jovelyn Magay is one of…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The prosecution panel on Tuesday is set to present its first reserved witness to testify in Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial.
Police Maj. Jovelyn Magay is one of two reserved witnesses expected to testify for Article I, or Duterte’s alleged misuse of confidential funds.

While the prosecution refused to detail what it intended to present through Magay, its lead counsel, Rep. Gerville Luistro, said Magay would testify on the acknowledgment receipts that the Office of the Vice President (OVP) and the Department of Education (DepEd) submitted to the Commission on Audit (COA) as proof of CF disbursement.

Previously, defense lead counsel Sheila Sison took issue with the lack of details the prosecution gave about Magay’s possible testimony, saying the defense panel would have no prior preparation without a description of the “surprise witness.”
In response, Luistro assured that the prosecution would present its offer of testimony before it begins examining Magay, clarifying that she is an “additional witness.”

Though the defense was seemingly unsatisfied with this response, Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero said the court would give the defense ample time to prepare for its cross-examination of Magay.
After Magay, the prosecution is expected to call to the stand DepEd Assistant Secretary Sunshine Fajarda, wife of former DepEd special disbursing officer Edward Fajarda.
The Fajarda couple supposedly had a close relationship with Duterte, which began in 2011 when Duterte was mayor of Davao City.

Edward Fajarda turned over DepEd confidential funds to Duterte’s security detail when she was still Education chief. He was supposed to be another witness for the prosecution but was withdrawn after suffering a stroke and requiring a month-long recovery.
The couple are also Duterte’s co-respondents in the Office of the Ombudsman proceedings for plunder, malversation of public funds, and related offenses.
Fajarda’s testimony will be followed by that of the prosecution’s second reserved witness, COA Intelligence and Confidential Funds Audit Office Assistant Commissioner Bresilio Sabaldan.
Like Magay, the prosecution did not disclose ahead of time what testimony Sabaldan may offer during the trial.

But two COA-ICFAO auditors, Roderick Wamil and Xylene del Campo, already testified that in auditing Duterte’s P612.5 million in CFs for DepEd and the OVP, they flagged discrepancies such as a lack of supporting documents and noncompliance with the proper use of CFs. /mcm

articles.title: Remains of missing man found near river in Benguet town
articles.summary: BAGUIO CITY — Search and rescue teams on Monday (September 7) have recovered the remains of a 29-year-old Kibungan town resident of Barangay Sagubo in Benguet province, who had been missing since…

blocks.text: BAGUIO CITY — Search and rescue teams on Monday (September 7) have recovered the remains of a 29-year-old Kibungan town resident of Barangay Sagubo in Benguet province, who had been missing since September 3.

Raul Aludos Juan was found at around 2 p.m. in the Sagilic area of Kaliwaga, Barangay Gaswiling, along the Manahongkong River, according to the Kapangan Municipal Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (MDRRMO).
Juan’s remains were brought to his home in Barangay Sagubo, where his family will make arrangements for his funeral.

Juan was reported missing to the Kapangan MDRRMO on September 5, prompting an initial search by barangay officials and community volunteers. The municipal disaster office later activated its search and rescue team and coordinated with other responding agencies and the La Union towns of Bagulin and Naguilian.

Based on the initial reports, the individual might have been swept away by water current along the river between the boundary of Gaswiling and Sagubo. Authorities believe the individual went to the river to catch fish as fishing equipment were later found in the area. /jpv

articles.title: Trump threatens to stop sale of Canadian Bombardier jets in US
articles.summary: The threat against one of Canada's largest companies comes amid an escalating trade war between the two neighbours.

blocks.text: President Donald Trump has warned Canadian aircraft company Bombardier that it can no longer sell in the US unless it moves its manufacturing there.
"NO MORE SELLING BOMBARDIER IN THE UNITED STATES!" Trump wrote in a Truth Social post on Monday. "If they want our Market, they must build here, and stop treating America like a 'piggybank.'"
The move comes amid an escalating trade war between the two neighbours, and hours before Canadian retaliatory tariffs are set to be imposed on $20bn (£14.7) worth of US goods.
The BBC has contacted Prime Minister Mark Carney's office and Bombardier for comment.
It is unclear how Trump intends to block Bombardier from doing business in the US.
The Montreal-based company already operates a factory in the US state of Kansas that builds special mission military planes, and employs 3,500 American workers.
About half of its fleet – 5,100 aircraft – is operated by Bombardier customers based in the US.

Bombardier's jets are built at facilities in Canada, the US and Mexico, according to the company's website. They also comply with the North American free trade agreement signed by Trump during his first term, known as CUSMA in Canada and the USMCA in the US.
The company is one of Canada's largest, having contributed C$7.4bn ($5.4bn; £4bn) to the country's GDP in 2024, according to a report commissioned by Bombardier.
It is also one of the largest employers in Quebec's manufacturing sector.
In a post on X on Monday, Quebec premier Christine Fréchette called the company "a source of pride" for her province and "a flagship of our economy".
She added that she has reached out to Bombardier CEO Éric Martel and offered her government's full support.
On Trump's threat, Fréchette wrote: "I will not respond to provocation with provocation."
"Quebec will not allow anyone to dictate where our companies must produce in order to access a market."
Trade talks between Canada and the US collapsed late last month after Canada walked away from the negotiating table, after which the US imposed new 50% tariffs on a range of Canadian goods.

Prime Minister Carney accused the Trump administration of presenting last-minute terms that were "unfair" and "uneconomic", while US officials accused him of refusing to sign a deal for political reasons because of Trump's unpopularity in Canada - an accusation he denied.

articles.title: Canada’s retaliatory US tariffs set to take effect as trade dispute grows
articles.summary:
Counter-measures covering several sectors come after Trump announced 50% tariffs on Canadian goods

Canada is set to impose retaliatory tariffs on billions of dollars’ worth of American…

blocks.text: Canada is set to impose retaliatory tariffs on billions of dollars’ worth of American imports early on Tuesday, escalating a trade fight with its largest trading partner as tensions between US president Donald Trump and Canadian prime minister Mark Carney intensify.

The tariffs, which take effect at 12.01am on Tuesday, will range from 15% to 50% and apply to products covering C$27.6bn in imports from the US. The measures will target sectors including steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics – industries that have been most affected by US tariffs.
The retaliatory tariffs come “as a result of the United States’ decision to impose a 50% tariff on $27.6bn of Canadian goods effective August 22”, the Canadian government said.
“Canada’s counter-measures do not apply to US goods that are in transit to Canada on the day on which they come into force,” it added.

Tensions between Canada and the US have intensified in recent weeks, with Carney last week urging the Trump administration to “start being serious” as the trade dispute has increasingly spilled into broader diplomatic tensions.

Trump and senior US officials have repeatedly criticized Canada and its leadership, while Trump has taken a series of symbolic digs at Canada including signing an executive order renaming Lake Ontario “Lake America” – which Canadians have rejected.
US vice-president JD Vance has also reportedly mocked Carney, apparently saying the Canadian prime minister “comes in and puffs his chest out and says: ‘I’m going to, like, out-tough Donald Trump.’”
Last month, Trump announced a new 50% tariff on cars and raw materials from Canada. He accused the country of “ripping off” the US “for years”, adding: “We don’t need Canada, they need us!”

Carney said last month Canada would not accept a US trade deal that weakened French-language protections, saying American negotiators viewed the measures as an “irritant”, while “in Quebec, these are rights”.

Quebec has long maintained laws aimed at protecting French and preserving its distinct cultural identity. Those measures have become a sticking point in the trade talks between the two countries, with American negotiators raising concerns about rules they say can disadvantage US businesses.
