This came days after Reiner Novero, 25, died after falling into a flooded, open drainage canal along the Fil-Am Friendship Highway in Barangay Cutcut in Angeles City, Pampanga, on Aug. 28. He was swept away by the floodwaters when he fell.

Novero’s body was found beneath a bridge in front of a subdivision in Barangay Sto. Domingo, some two kilometers from where he fell. The incident sparked safety concerns among many social media users pointing out why a drainage canal was left open.

Meanwhile, Environment Secretary Juan Miguel Cuna announced the rollout of the Provincial Climate Risk Diagnostics (PCRD) tool to more provinces to help local governments spot risks and build resilience from natural disasters.

Developed with the United Nations and the Department of Human Settlements and Urban Development, the tool helps identify risks from climate hazards, such as flooding, landslides, severe winds, forest fires and extreme temperatures.

“Climate action is strongest when it is guided by sound data and risk-informed planning,” Cuna said in a statement, stressing that this will help local governments transition toward evidence-based decisions that protect communities, sustain livelihoods and safeguard ecosystems.
After all, local governments need to base adaptation and development decisions on reliable evidence, he added.
The tool can also assess current conditions and projected exposure scenarios for 2030 and 2050, giving provinces information needed to develop long-term adaptation strategies.
El Niño
Earlier, the United Nations’ weather agency warned that El Niño is expected to intensify to “very strong” levels in the coming months and is almost certain to persist through February.

El Niño raises sea-surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, triggering changes in global wind patterns, atmospheric pressure, and rainfall. The World Meteorological Organization said the phenomenon is likely to peak toward the end of the year, with its climate impacts expected to linger into 2027. —WITH A REPORT FROM SHERIDAN DELFINO

articles.title: Social media posts reveal wider habitat of Philippine tarsiers
articles.summary: With their huge eyes and bodies small enough to fit in the palm of a hand, Philippine tarsiers are among the best-known inhabitants of the country’s tropical forests. The tiny nocturnal primates are…

blocks.text: With their huge eyes and bodies small enough to fit in the palm of a hand, Philippine tarsiers are among the best-known inhabitants of the country’s tropical forests.

The tiny nocturnal primates are closely associated with the central island of Bohol, a popular tourist destination, but researchers have found evidence that their range is far more extensive than previously documented.

A study by researchers at the University of the Philippines Diliman found reports of Philippine tarsiers in 29 provinces, more than double the 14 provinces previously identified as habitats by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN).
The findings were based largely on an unlikely source: Facebook.

Graduate student Simeon Bejar, 30, and fellow researcher Maria Tabeta, 25, examined more than 1,000 Facebook posts dating back to 2006, gathering information on tarsier sightings and analyzing where photographs of the animals had been posted.
More habitats
The IUCN had previously identified tarsier habitats in just 14 of the Philippines’ 82 provinces.
They also found numerous sightings in northern Leyte and indications that forests there may have tarsier population densities comparable to those in protected areas in Bohol.
“I think it’s really appropriate to do it here because a lot of Filipinos use Facebook,” Bejar said.
More than 80 percent of the Philippine population is estimated to use Facebook, giving the researchers a vast pool of information posted by people across the archipelago of more than 7,000 islands.

The Philippine tarsier, an endemic species measuring little more than 10 centimeters in body length, is difficult to find because of its small size and nocturnal habits. Much about its ecology remains unknown.
It is classified as “Near Threatened” on the IUCN Red List.
The study also highlighted shortcomings in efforts to protect the animals.
On Bohol, where ecotourism is a major attraction, the Department of Environment and Natural Resources and local authorities have stepped up management of forests inhabited by tarsiers.
Protected areas open to tourists have also introduced rules aimed at minimizing stress on the animals, including asking visitors to keep their voices down.
But the researchers found signs of problems elsewhere.
“Some of the Facebook posts featured photographs of tarsiers being inside cages, which is illegal. Some are leashed … some were dead,” Bejar said.
Illegal trafficking
Illegal trafficking for the pet trade is one of the main threats facing Philippine tarsiers, and poaching appears to be taking place in areas beyond the reach of authorities.
Bejar and Tabeta have set up a dedicated Facebook page for their research and hope to expand the scale of the study.
“If maybe we get another student who can work with us or a project where we can use funds to focus on this, then we’ll try to scale up what we are doing right now,” Bejar said.—KYODO NEWS

articles.title: Palestinian parents fear for children's lives at school as settler attacks grow
articles.summary: A headteacher in the occupied West Bank has installed new barbed wire fencing after three pupils were killed this year.

blocks.text: On the first day of the new Palestinian school year, the head-teacher of al-Mughayyir boys school arrived at work before dawn, walking past the freshly installed barbed wire fencing and reinforced school gates as the sun began creeping through olive trees around the village, deep inside the occupied West Bank.
"We are scared," Bassam al Assaf told me. "The students are afraid, and their parents are afraid."

Six people, including three pupils at the school, have been killed in al-Mughayyir this year, in a surge of settler-related violence against Palestinians. One of them, 14-year-old Aws al-Naasan, was shot dead by a settler outside the school gates in April.

"I was inside my classroom and two little students came rushing to tell me there were settlers close to the school wall," remembers English teacher Waheed Abu Naem, whose brother Jihad was also killed by an Israeli soldier in the same attack.
Waheed said he was trying to move pupils to safety inside the school gate when the settler fired towards them. Mobile phone footage shows the moment Aws was shot.
"When I turned him onto his back, I saw lots of blood coming from his nose and mouth, and the bullet in his head," said Waheed. "We lost him."
He told me that bullets continued hitting the school building, as students hid behind the walls of their classrooms, or lay on the floor.

The Israeli military said in a statement at the time that stones had been hurled at a car carrying "civilians including a reservist soldier", and that the reservist had got out of the vehicle and fired at suspects.
Israeli media reported the reservist was later suspended from duty and an investigation launched.
Since that day, the casualties have grown alongside parents' fears.
Over the summer, two more pupils were shot dead by Israeli forces during settler attacks and incursions in the village, along with a 19-year-old who had just left the school.
In both cases, Israel's army said its forces responded to instigators of "a violent riot".
With three empty desks in the classrooms, some parents were reluctant to send their children back for the new school year.

The school sits right on the edge of Al-Mughayyir, an isolated village north-east of Ramallah, increasingly surrounded by Jewish settler outposts, and regularly blocked by Israeli forces who frequently operate an ad-hoc checkpoint at the entrance.

Bassam al-Assaf has installed a long barbed-wire fence around the compound and reinforced the school gates, to try and reassure parents. Ambulance crews are now stationed on the road outside, and several parents have volunteered to wait outside the school all day as an extra layer of protection.
"I came because it makes the children feel their parents are with them, that they are safe, it gives them a kind of security," said Haroon Bishara, whose boys are in the first and second grades.
"We fear for our children more this year," he told me. "We know the situation is not safe at the school."
But he said that fear was mixed with a determination not to let the threat from settler attacks force them out.

Lined up in the playground for their first assembly, pupils heard the instructions repeated by teachers again and again throughout the day: if soldiers or settlers approach the school, don't shout, don't go near them, don't react.

Just over an hour after classes began, settlers were spotted through the school windows: two men, driving sheep through Palestinian fields a couple of hundred metres from the school, as Israeli soldiers stood close by.
Minutes later, another settler with a flock of sheep appeared.
"They have got closer to the village since April," said Abu Naem. They used to keep their sheep behind this [hill], but now the soldiers bring the settlers up to the village."
We asked the Israeli army for its response to all the allegations in this report, but they were unable to provide one before publication.

All Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank are illegal under international law. Many of the small ad-hoc settler outposts that have mushroomed around al-Mughayyir are illegal under Israeli law too.
But one of the ambulance crews stationed outside the school said that, rather than remove illegal settlements, Israeli soldiers had begun supporting and enabling settler incursions into the village.

Hadi al-Naasan, an ambulance driver in the village, said there had been a shift in the behaviour of Israeli forces over the past year. And that the rise in Palestinian deaths and injuries in al-Mughayyir this year reflected that.

"At the beginning of 2025, settler attacks were few, due to the army's interventions," he said. "In 2026, the situation changed completely: the settlers became fully protected by the occupation soldiers. This year, the number of martyrs is higher, the number of injuries is also much higher – and the number of child injuries is higher too."

Hadi, along with other residents of al-Mughayyir, believes that some Israeli settlers are now deliberately targeting children in order to put pressure on the adults in the village to leave their homes.
A UN Commission of Inquiry published in June found that settler attacks "have instrumentalized children, external as part of a broader coercive strategy to drive Palestinians off their land."

And it described "a pattern of settlers intentionally targeting Palestinian children" while they were playing near their homes, walking to and from school, tending to farms or herding livestock, "turning everyday spaces into sites of fear".
Israel dismissed the report as a "libellous sham".
Sheep farmer Sami Abu Rahma firmly believes that some violent settlers are targeting children.
At the end of July, his nine-year-old son Salim was shot and injured as he played with his siblings on the family sheep farm outside al-Mughayyir. The bullet is still lodged in his arm.

Footage from security cameras at the farm shows Salim pointing, and shouting to his parents that settlers are approaching, before running for shelter with his siblings and mother, as two gunshots are heard. Salim is seen grabbing his shoulder.

"In that moment, you stop thinking; you just feel fear," Sami told me. "Fear that, God forbid, [the attacker] was shooting to kill. The first thing in your mind is losing the most precious thing you have."
The man who shot his son, he said, lived in an illegal settler outpost that appeared next to the farm in June – and had previously shot at Salim in the same area a week before.
"You no longer feel you can keep them safe in the street, or even at school," he said. "The settlers don't want us to stay here, [they want us to feel] as if there's no future for us here."
Sami said he was the last sheep farmer left in the area, the others all chased away by settler attacks. The settler who shot his son had told the family repeatedly to leave their land, he said.
"No matter how determined you might be to stay," he added, "what do you do when settlers start shooting your kids?"
The regional settlers council told us that an off-duty soldier was arrested on suspicion of involvement in the shooting.

"We regret any harm to innocent people, Jews or Arabs, and oppose any act of violence that violates the law," it said in a statement, adding that it rejected "the attempt to attribute to the entire settlement community in Judea and Samaria acts that have not yet been determined by an investigation, as well as the baseless claim that lawful sheep grazing or Jewish presence in the area are part of a deliberate plan to harm children or drive residents from their homes."

Al-Mughayyir is part of a pattern unfolding across the occupied West Bank, with more illegal settler outposts encircling Palestinian villages, more protection for settlers from Israeli forces, and attacks moving from farms and grazing land to built-up areas, where women and children are more at risk.
"Children, seeing the army enter, don't grasp the gravity of the situation," said the local ambulance crew, Hadi al-Naasan. "Adults are more aware of how events can unfold."

UN figures suggest that the number of Palestinians injured during settler attacks by Israeli soldiers or settlers has risen sharply this year to an average of three injuries per day, and that the number of injuries inflicted directly by settlers themselves is also higher.
This rise has been accompanied by an expansion of Israeli settlements and settler outposts in the West Bank.

All Israeli settlements in the West Bank are illegal under international law, and Israel's fiercely pro-settlement government is under growing international pressure - including from the UK, which is expected to announce sanctions this week in response to Israeli settlement policies.

The arrest of some violent settlers and a reported plan by Israel's prime minister to dismantle illegal outposts in the West Bank have not so far stopped attacks, nor reassured Palestinians who say outposts previously demolished by Israeli authorities were quickly rebuilt.

With Israeli elections less than two months away, Israel's Finance Ministry pushed forward plans this week to take over land registration in the West Bank and East Jerusalem, described by the Israeli settlement monitor Peace Now as "a clear step towards annexation".
Israel's prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has attributed settler violence to a tiny extremist minority, describing them in a recent television interview as "150 juvenile delinquents".

Since the beginning of 2025, the UN has recorded 316 Palestinians killed by Israeli forces or settlers, and more than 5,600 injured, to the end of July 2026. It says 20 Israelis were killed over the same period, including one child and eight members of the security forces, and 123 Israelis injured.
Palestinian parents who have stayed in villages like al-Mughayyir through escalating settler violence are now facing a growing fear of losing their children if they stay on their land.

articles.title: Biocontrol fungi help curb RSSI in Negros fields
articles.summary: BACOLOD CITY—Biocontrol materials produced by the provincial government of Negros Occidental have shown positive results against the red-striped soft scale insect (RSSI) in treated sugarcane fields.…

blocks.text: BACOLOD CITY—Biocontrol materials produced by the provincial government of Negros Occidental have shown positive results against the red-striped soft scale insect (RSSI) in treated sugarcane fields.

Provincial Administrator Rayfrando Diaz II said field observations and initial laboratory tests confirmed the presence and effectiveness of the province-produced biological controls, two months after the creation of the provincial task force against RSSI.

Field samples collected from sugarcane farms in Caliban, Murcia, showed RSSI cadavers infected with entomopathogenic fungi, with visible fungal spores growing on the dead insects, Diaz said in an advisory on Saturday.

The biocontrol materials were first applied in the fields on Aug. 14. Three weeks after the application, the beneficial fungi had become established in the fields and were affecting RSSI populations, he said.
Science-based efforts
Diaz said the preliminary field and laboratory findings support the province’s continuing science-based efforts to contain the spread of the pest and protect Negros Occidental’s sugarcane industry.
The provincial government, led by Gov. Eugenio Jose Lacson, continues to develop and distribute biocontrol materials while expanding its production capacity, Diaz said. —CARLA P. GOMEZ INQ

articles.title: Sea inches closer as dredging worries Zambales folk
articles.summary: SAN FELIPE, ZAMBALES—For 52-year-old Myra Falloran, her family home in Sitio (subvillage) Tektek, Barangay Sindol, was meant to be an inheritance for her grandchildren. Now, the sea is creeping…

blocks.text: SAN FELIPE, ZAMBALES—For 52-year-old Myra Falloran, her family home in Sitio (subvillage) Tektek, Barangay Sindol, was meant to be an inheritance for her grandchildren.
Now, the sea is creeping closer.
Falloran said the shoreline began changing after dredging activities started in 2022. The operation was halted at one point but resumed in October 2023.

Dredging in Zambales was conducted under Department of Environment and Natural Resources Administrative Order No. 13 to clear silted river channels and help prevent flooding. But residents, particularly fishermen, questioned the presence of 17 Chinese dredging vessels in San Felipe’s municipal waters.

The provincial government the suspended dredging in March 2025 following protests but lifted the suspension in June. Operations resumed in the Sto. Tomas and Bucao rivers, while the Maloma River remained suspended.
Falloran said the shoreline continued to erode, with waves now reaching homes during high tide.
“We can really feel the difference because this did not happen before. The sea would naturally come closer, but it never reached our homes,” she told the Inquirer.
Erosion
Falloran said she supported dredging for flood prevention but opposed offshore operations and the lack of consultation.
“But I wish they had limited the dredging to the mouth of the river, not in the sea directly in front of our homes,” she said.
Falloran blamed the removal of sand for the erosion.
“If they had not taken the sand, this would not have happened,” she said.
Her concerns come as heavy rains again displaced residents across Zambales. The provincial disaster office reported 604 families, or 1,854 people, evacuated as of Monday.
Falloran said flooding and damage to the coastal road have also affected fishermen’s livelihoods.
“I hope the damaged coastal road can also be rehabilitated soon … because there is no longer any place for our boats to be launched,” she said.
She appealed for long-term protection and livelihood assistance instead of temporary relief. INQ

articles.title: Adult dugong dies as juvenile rescued in Antique
articles.summary: ILOILO CITY, Philippines — An adult dugong was found dead along the coast of Sebaste, Antique, on Monday, a day after residents rescued a stranded juvenile of the threatened marine mammal in…

blocks.text: ILOILO CITY—An adult dugong was found dead along the coast of Sebaste, Antique, on Monday, a day after residents rescued a stranded juvenile of the threatened marine mammal in neighboring Caluya town.
The adult dugong was found along the shoreline of Barangay Aras-Asan, where authorities examined the carcass and arranged for its proper handling.

Flord Nicson Calawag, a licensed fisheries technologist and biodiversity researcher, said the dugong appeared to be a large adult based on photographs, but its cause of death could not be determined without a necropsy.
He said strong waves brought by the southwest monsoon, or “habagat,” may have washed the carcass ashore, but this would not establish what caused the animal’s death.
A necropsy could determine whether the dugong died from fishing-related injuries, marine debris, vessel collision, disease or other natural or human-related causes, Calawag said.

The discovery came a day after residents helped a juvenile dugong that became stranded in shallow water during low tide on Liwagao Island in Barangay Sibolo, Caluya. The animal was successfully returned to the sea on Sunday (Sept. 6).
Stranded
There was no indication that the two incidents were related.
Dugongs depend largely on seagrass meadows in shallow coastal waters and face threats including accidental capture in fishing gear, vessel strikes and habitat loss.

The dugong is classified as Critically Endangered under the Philippines’ national conservation assessment, while the International Union for Conservation of Nature lists the species as Vulnerable globally.
Authorities urged the public to avoid disturbing stranded dugongs and other marine wildlife and to report sightings to the proper authorities.

articles.title: Tokyo’s Shinjuku Ward to ban vacation rentals
articles.summary: Tokyo’s Shinjuku Ward plans to ban, as a general rule, vacation rentals such as Airbnbs in residential areas and areas near schools, local officials said on Monday. The ward in central Tokyo hosts…

blocks.text: Tokyo’s Shinjuku Ward plans to ban, as a general rule, vacation rentals such as Airbnbs in residential areas and areas near schools, local officials said on Monday.
The ward in central Tokyo hosts the largest concentration of vacation rentals in the country. The policy will also apply to existing properties, the officials said.

There were 3,775 registered short-term rental properties in the ward as of July 15, according to the Japan Tourism Agency. The ward estimates that approximately 2,000 of them may have to cease operations under the plan.

The agency and other relevant bodies notified local governments in July that they could effectively ban short-term rentals in specific areas through local ordinances if the properties were found to be harming the residential environment, citing a series of incidents.
The ward plans to solicit public comments in October and submit an amendment to its short-term rental ordinance at the first regular session of the ward assembly in February next year.
According to the officials, the ban will apply to areas zoned for residential use only or designated as cultural and educational districts.
Exceptions will be made for vacation rentals that meet certain requirements, such as those whose owners live on-site and manage the properties appropriately. —KYODO NEWS

articles.title: Cardinal Tagle’s father; 96
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The 96-year-old father of Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle died on Sunday, Sept. 6. Manuel Tagle Sr., who celebrated his 70th wedding anniversary with his wife, Milagros, last…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The 96-year-old father of Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle died on Sunday, Sept. 6.

Manuel Tagle Sr., who celebrated his 70th wedding anniversary with his wife, Milagros, last August, passed away at 7:09 a.m. CBCP News said the cardinal, who is currently serving as proprefect of the Vatican’s Dicastery for Evangelization, was in Rome when his father breathed his last.

As stated in the report, Tagle said they thanked God for his father’s life and mission as he asked for prayers for his eternal repose: “May Tatay Maning rest in peace, with Mary, the angels and saints.”
The wake and viewing at Casas Hall in the Bishop’s House in Imus City, Cavite, began on Sept. 7 and ends on Sept. 9. Visits are from 7 a.m. to 10 p.m.
The Requiem Mass will be held at 10 a.m. on Sept. 10 at Imus Cathedral. —KURT DELA PEÑA

articles.title: Australia politics live: John Howard warns about limiting immigration; Barnaby Joyce says super plan to have ‘minute’ inflationary effect
articles.summary:
Follow the day’s news live

Former prime minister, John Howard, has warned political parties against banning migration from certain countries as the

blocks.text: John Howard says blocking immigration from certain countries won't stop terrorism
The former prime minister John Howard has warned political parties against banning migration from certain countries as the debate over Australia’s immigration settings continues.

The 87-year-old was in Canberra last night for an hour-long chat with Australian National University national security professor Rory Medcalf before the 25th anniversary of the September 11 terrorist attacks in the US.
The discussion began with last year’s alleged terrorist attack in Bondi, before turning to whether immigration settings can prevent potential terrorists from entering the country.
Howard said the “law of averages” meant some people with nefarious intentions could enter the country but he did not believe the “evidence is overwhelming”.
He continued:

double quotation markBut I think the mood is overwhelming that we have to try very hard to stop terrorism creeping in under the cover of immigration, and you can’t do it by just stopping immigration, and it’s very hard to do it by stopping categories of immigration. When some people say you stop it by saying ‘we won’t take migrants from any country that has got a reputation for terrorism’, well, it might be a lot more limiting than those people imagine.

Neither major political party has proposed a country-wide ban on specific countries for permanent migration. One Nation has said it would like to see country-wide migration bans on people coming from countries the foreign affairs department has listed as “do not travel”.
Key events

items: 17m agoGood morning
17m agoJoyce says super plan has 'minute' inflationary effect
17m agoJohn Howard says blocking immigration from certain countries won't stop terrorism

blocks.text: Joyce says super plan has 'minute' inflationary effect

One Nation’s deputy leader, Barnaby Joyce, has defended his party’s new policy allowing renters and mortgage holders to dip into their superannuation to boost their pay, saying it will have a “minute” impact on inflation.

The superannuation industry has warned the policy – which Labor and the Coalition have said they do not support – would stoke inflation. The Association of Superannuation Funds of Australia chief executive, Mary Delahunty, said the proposal would be “economically disastrous” and make people poorer in retirement.

Speaking to the ABC’s 7.30 on Monday night, Joyce – the party’s Treasury spokesperson – said withdrawing your superannuation from your fund due to financial hardship was currently a “protracted” system.
Asked if the party had modelled the inflationary impact of the policy, Joyce said it would have a minimal impact but did not point to any modelling:
double quotation markNow are you saying that it has no effect whatsoever? No, I wouldn’t say that but I’d say it is almost minute.
Joyce says allegations against Victorian One Nation leader are ‘contested’
Barnaby Joyce was also asked about One Nation’s Victorian leader, Warren Pickering, who continues to attract scrutiny over allegations made against him by an ex-partner about alleged drug use.
Pickering said his ex-partner’s claims were false. “They are extremely hurtful and I just hope the public can see through them,” he said in a statement, according to The Australian.
Speaking to the ABC’s 7.30, Joyce said the historical allegations were “contested”.
He said he did not hear about the allegations before story was published in The Australian on Monday:

double quotation markIf he’s good enough to serve our nation in the defence force, as determined by our nation, then I presume he’s good enough to serve the people of Victoria. If we’re saying that any person will be held to account for any action they ever did, no matter how far in the past it was, I would suggest there are lot of people in this parliament who will no longer have a job Monday morning.
Good morning
Welcome to Guardian Australia’s live news coverage for Tuesday.
Krishani Dhanji will be with you shortly.
Let’s begin.

articles.title: Giuliani says Mamdani should skip 9/11 ceremony during rant against Islam
articles.summary:
New York City mayor confirms he will attend memorial service but declines to respond to Giuliani’s remarks

New York mayor Zohran…

blocks.text: New York mayor Zohran Mamdani is set to come face-to-face with Rudy Giuliani at the main September 11 memorial service, just days after the former mayor – who led the city at the time of the 2001 terrorist attacks – disparaged his Muslim religion and said he should skip the ceremony.
In an interview with right-leaning Newsmax at the weekend, Giuliani said: “Having lost friends there and being very close to many of the families, it offends me that he’s coming.”

Mamdani confirmed on Monday, while attending a breakfast celebrating New York’s J’ouvert and West Indian Day Parade celebrations in Brooklyn, that he will attend the main ceremony and multiple 9/11 events on Friday, to stand with the families of those who died and first responders – as he did last year before taking office.

“I’m proud to be the mayor of this city. I love this city. I love this country,” he said. “What I want this week to be a focus on is on the families whose loved ones were stolen from them 25 years ago in the horrific act of terror of September 11th, and a focus also on the first responders who did everything they could.”
The mayor and his office have declined to respond to Giuliani’s remarks.

The former mayor and close ally of Donald Trump has said he will also attend this year’s ceremony to mark the attacks by Islamist terrorists representing al-Qaida, who flew hijacked passenger planes into the twin towers of the World Trade Center in lower Manhattan on September 11, 2001.

Reflecting pools with waterfalls constructed on the footprints of the towers and a 9/11 museum now mark the site that was dubbed Ground Zero in the aftermath of the attacks, and where each year the names of the almost 3,000 people who died are read out by survivors and loved ones, in a solemn ceremony attended by national and local leaders.

In the interview with Newsmax, Giuliani was asked if Mamdani should skip the ceremony. “Well, there’s no question he should,” he said. Giuliani was mayor of New York City from 1994 to 2001. He ran unsuccessfully for president and, more recently, has been an attorney to and a staunch ally of Donald Trump.

In the convoluted tirade on air on Saturday, Giuliani threw insults and baseless comparisons. He appeared to draw parallels between Mamdani’s faith and the 9/11 hijackers acting on the extremist orders of Osama bin Laden, the jihadist militant and terrorist leader killed by US forces during the Obama administration.

He remarked that the terrorists brought their ideological opposition to the United States “in the name of the Muslim religion” and “weren’t hiding it like Mamdani is trying to hide it”. He also declared the opinion that the mayor supports a notion that Islam should be the dominant religion.

Mamdani has previously spoken about how an Islamophobic backlash built after the 2001 attacks and had made anti-Muslim prejudice “a fact of life” for Muslim Americans. “It was this horrific day that was also, for many New Yorkers, the moment at which they were marked an ‘other’,” he told the New York Times last year.

Last week, Mamdani issued an executive order designating 9/11 an annual official “Day of Remembrance and Service” that requires the city administration to designate a moment of silence to mourn those who were killed and affected by the attacks. A second order established a new taskforce to help the city’s emergency preparedness.

Several high-profile figures, including Giuliani and former New York governor George Pataki have voiced opposition to Mamdani’s attendance at the ceremony, and an online petition arguing the same has gathered close to 100,000 signatures.

Dignitaries expected to attend Friday’s commemorations include former US presidents Bill Clinton, George W Bush and Barack Obama, and some other former mayors of New York. The White House has said Donald Trump is not attending but is expected to commemorate the 9/11 attack on the Pentagon at that site close to Washington DC, a decision that also has also drawn criticism. US vice-president JD Vance is expected to represent the White House in New York.

articles.title: Grindr to pay $48-million settlement over sale of users' info — including HIV status
articles.summary: The hookup app Grindr is on the hook for a huge payout after settling a U.K. lawsuit that alleged sensitive information about its users — including their HIV status — was sold to advertisers.

image.caption: The U.S.-owned app Grindr has reached a settlement in a U.K. lawsuit over claims it sold highly sensitive user data to advertising companies. (Martin Bureau/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Business·New
The hookup app Grindr is on the hook for a huge payout after settling a U.K. lawsuit that alleged sensitive information about its users — including their HIV status — was sold to advertisers.
Hookup app accused of violating U.K. privacy law by selling sensitive data to third parties
The California-based company agreed last week to pay £26 million (approximately $48.6 million Cdn) to some 12,000 people who signed up to the claim filed by London law firm Austen Hays in 2024.

The claim alleges Grindr violated U.K. privacy protection laws for a period prior to April 2020, when Grindr updated its consent guidelines, by sharing data with other companies in exchange for payment or commercial benefits.

items: How AI is infiltrating the dating world, from crafting flirty messages to matchmaking

blocks.text: That data included users' HIV status, most recent HIV testing dates and result and whether or not they were using PrEP, an HIV prevention regimen.
Such information is provided voluntarily by users and they can choose whether or not to display it publicly on their profiles.

Such information, the lawsuit claims, was shared with third parties, including the advertising companies Localytics and Apptimize, which would then allow ads to be targeted or customized based on the users' info. That data may have also been sold to fourth parties, the lawsuit claims.
"Grindr users may have assumed that the information submitted to the app was only available to other app users," Austen Hays says on its website.

The firm says Grindr "plays an important role" in the 2SLGBTQ+ community, facilitating dates and sexual encounters for gay, bisexual, trans and queer adults, and that it must "be held accountable and reinstate confidence in the way it treats user data."
Eligible claimants who used the free version of the app between 2016 and 2020 will be entitled to £2,167, or $4,050 Cdn each, if paid equally.

According to a U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filing posted Thursday, the publicly traded company will pay out the first half of the settlement by the end of this year, and the remainder by March 31, 2027.
CBC's Aarti Pole speaks to anthropologist Treena Orchard about a decline in dating apps
A 'loss of trust' for Grindr users
Per the SEC filing, Grindr says that "the settlement includes no findings or admission of liability."
"While Grindr disputes the allegations, it recognizes and acknowledges the distress and loss of trust expressed by some of its U.K. users regarding that pre-2020 period," the company said.

The British lawsuit followed Norway's government fining Grindr 100 million Norwegian kroner in 2021 — nearly $15 million Cdn at the time — for illegally sharing the data of users of the free version of the app.
Grindr challenged Norway's decision but lost its appeal in 2024.

items: Grindr says it will no longer share users' HIV status with outside companies (2018)
Grindr fraudster violates probation order after posing as a university professor (2024)

blocks.text: Grindr, which bills itself as the world's largest social networking app for 2SLGBTQ+ people, was solely owned by Chinese gaming company Beijing Kunlun Tech Co. Ltd. between 2018 and 2020. That company also held a majority stake since 2016.
The U.S. government ordered Kunlun to divest from the company over concerns about its handling of sensitive data like HIV status, as well as the contents of users' private messages.
A group of private investors known as San Vicente Acquisition LLC purchased Grindr for $620 million US, which the government approved in 2020.
Reuters later reported that investors involved in the San Vicente Acquisition group's purchase had ties to Kunlun.
Grindr was first launched in 2009 and claims to have more than 15 million monthly active users worldwide.
In its latest investor report, Grindr state it brought in $138 million US ($190 million CAD) in revenue in the second quarter of 2026.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Nick Logan is a senior writer with CBC based in Vancouver. He is a multi-platform reporter and producer, with a particular focus on international news. You can reach out to him at nick.logan@cbc.ca.
With files from Reuters

King Charles authorized a letter to senior British officials on Monday confirming that his youngest son, Prince Harry, and Harry's ‌wife, Meghan, remain non-working royals following their return to the U.K.
Couple stepped down from duties and moved to the U.S. in 2020

The letter, which was shared with Harry's team and sent as guidance to senior officials ​in the government and military, said that after ​Harry and Meghan stepped down from official royal duties in 2020, they "are no longer working Members ​of The Royal Family."

"This position, distinct from the State ⁠and Royal duties undertaken ⁠by the working Royal ‌Family, and with the personal latitude it brings the couple in respect of financial independence and protection of their privacy as they would wish, will continue to be ⁠fully respected," the letter said.

"It follows that there is no change to the current status of the Duke and Duchess of ‌Sussex.... The charitable work of the Duke and Duchess is a personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity.
"In short, their position is akin to ​private citizens with commercial and charitable interests."

items: The 'shockwaves' of Prince Harry and Meghan's return to the U.K.

blocks.text: Prince Harry and his family arrived ⁠back in Britain late last month, six years after quitting royal ⁠duties and moving to the United States.

The couple had left ⁠for ⁠the U.S. in 2020, ​stepping down from official royal duties to chart independent careers, but ​they never left the ⁠headlines as Harry accused the royals of neglect, the tabloid press of ruining his life and the government of failing to provide enough security for him to ever return home.

articles.title: Senate OKs five international resolutions on third reading
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Senate on Monday approved, on its third and final reading, five international resolutions on aviation security, criminal justice cooperation, space activities, higher…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Senate on Monday approved, on its third and final reading, five international resolutions on aviation security, criminal justice cooperation, space activities, higher education, and taxation.
In a roll call vote, 19 senators, with no abstentions or objections, approved the following resolutions aimed at strengthening the Philippines’ participation in international agreements:

items: Senate Resolution No. 622, which seeks concurrence in the accession to the Protocol to Amend the Convention on Offenses and Certain Other Acts Committed on Board Aircraft, strengthening the legal framework for offenses committed aboard aircraft.

Senate Resolution No. 624, providing concurrence in the ratification of the Philippine-India Treaty on Mutual Legal Assistance in Criminal Matters, which establishes mechanisms for cooperation in investigating, prosecuting, and preventing crimes between India and the Philippines.

Senate Resolution No. 625, concurring in the ratification of the Convention on International Liability for Damage Caused by Space Objects, providing a framework for liability and compensation for damage caused by space objects.

Senate Resolution No. 626, which seeks concurrence in the Philippines’ accession to the Asia-Pacific Regional Convention on the Recognition of Qualifications in Higher Education, facilitating the recognition of Filipino academic qualifications abroad.

Senate Resolution No. 628, concurring in the ratification of the Philippines–Cambodia Agreement on the Elimination of Double Taxation and the Prevention of Fiscal Evasion with respect to Taxes on Income, which seeks to prevent double taxation and strengthen bilateral economic ties.

blocks.text: The approval of these measures is expected to improve the country’s cross-border cooperation while also supporting the country’s economic, educational, and security interests. /cb

articles.title: Police used batons and pepper spray on far-right protesters in Portsmouth unrest
articles.summary:
Minister condemns groups behind Hampshire disorder and says officers were injured as they repelled ‘aggression’

Batons and synthetic pepper spray were used to repel hundreds of masked,…
articles.byline: Rajeev Syal, Steven Morris and Ben Quinn

blocks.text: Batons and synthetic pepper spray were used to repel hundreds of masked, black-clad vigilantes in Portsmouth on Sunday, it has emerged, as the policing minister said officers had been injured as they repelled organised “aggression”.

After police contained the weekend’s second disruptive demonstration against asylum seekers travelling to the UK in small boats, it was claimed that officers in Hampshire were pushed off their motorbikes and pelted with bricks. Sarah Jones, the Home Office minister, condemned groups behind the disorder for promoting “racism and thuggery”.

Activists wearing balaclavas clashed with police in Portsmouth on Sunday evening after a dinghy reached the UK from Normandy. Hampshire and Isle of Wight constabulary have launched an investigation into potential assaults and criminal damage.
Daniel Thomas, a far-right agitator closely linked to Tommy Robinson, the longtime anti-Islam figure whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, claimed to have arranged the protest.
Thomas was also behind disruption in Dover on Saturday, when crowds of people dressed in black and wearing balaclavas blocked the road around the port for several hours.

blocks.caption: Daniel Thomas, left, speaking to the Reform UK home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf (right, in blue suit), has claimed to have arranged the demonstration. Photograph: Theo Shaw/PA

blocks.text: In a statement to MPs, Jones said: “Hampshire and Isle of Wight constabulary, with the support of other neighbouring forces, used a dispersal notice to ensure public safety and officers were forced to use batons and Pava spray to maintain order in the face of some aggression.”

Spencer Wragg, the chair of the Hampshire police federation, said one of the officers injured was a rookie who had only finished training school three days earlier. “Those scenes in that area of Portsmouth weren’t protests, they weren’t protests at all, it was clear that some people were intent on disorder and venting their frustrations,” he said.
About 120 people seeking asylum were brought to shore in Hampshire after travelling to the UK on a “mega-dinghy” which had departed from the Normandy coast and was at sea for roughly 10 hours.

The landing point of the dinghy was farther west than most small boat arrivals. Officials are concerned that people smugglers are starting to target new routes across England’s south coast, with craft launched from a wider stretch of the French shoreline.

blocks.caption: About 120 people seeking asylum were brought to shore in Hampshire at the weekend.  Photograph: Hannah McKay/Reuters

blocks.text: An estimated 200 protesters gathered, and clashed with riot police on Sunday night, vowing to prevent migrants leaving the port. Footage showed some chanting “send them back” as police officers with shields raised tried to maintain order.

Amid concerns that police were caught unawares by the unrest in Dover on Saturday, Jones said: “Work is ongoing to establish any lessons and ensure that relevant intelligence is shared at pace across our law enforcement system.”
Labour and Lib Dem MPs called on the government to explain why police appeared to have been caught off-guard by the events in Dover and Portsmouth.

Mike Tapp, the Labour MP for Dover and a former Home Office minister, questioned why the police were not aware of plans to block the local port. “Please ensure that the intelligence picture is strong enough so that the police can respond accordingly to future incidents,” he told MPs.

The Liberal Democrat Home Office spokesperson, Max Wilkinson, asked: “How is it that far-right thugs in balaclavas were able to close Britain’s busiest port without the police receiving any prior intelligence? And how is it that then an apparently separate group with some commonalities were then able to blockade another site the next evening?”

blocks.caption: Sarah Jones, the Home Office minister, said the government would learn lessons from the disorder. Photograph: House of Commons/UK Parliament/PA

blocks.text: Jones said there was “a crossover in terms of online activity” and the government would learn lessons from the disorder.

In an on-camera confrontation on Monday, Thomas, known as Danny Tommo, told the Reform UK home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, that the Patriot Platform group he led would deliver working-class votes to Reform – but expressed anger at Nigel Farage’s criticisms of Dover demonstrators for wearing balaclavas.

Thomas said: “I understand Nigel is going to be prime minister one day and I understand he has to set a standard, which will basically be that you know he can’t just come out and say, everything’s great and these guys are fantastic, but Nigel needs to be very careful with his words.”

Yusuf said he would “take that message back” and added that Thomas had articulated why he and his group had organised demonstrations. “I think it’s important we listen to people. He was making his points respectfully,” he said.
Police could impose a balaclava ban on future anti-migrant demonstrations after officers were injured, Whitehall sources said.

Under the Crime and Policing Act, Hampshire police could apply for a ban to ensure that protesters cannot cover their faces. Facebook posts claim that a demonstration is planned for Saturday by a group called Portsmouth Patriots. Hampshire police has been approached for comment.

Ministers have been criticised for failing to condemn far-right groups behind the disorder. Nick Lowles, the chief executive of Hope Not Hate, which charts far-right activity, told the BBC: “To have 300, 400 people with balaclavas marching down the streets, stopping traffic. You know, it’s not just good enough. We need to call these people out for their politics and for the type of Britain that they want to see.
“We’ve got different ways to register our protest. We do not go on the street. We do not burn people out of their houses. We do not cause trouble and threaten to fight the police.”

The Hampshire and Isle of Wight police and crime commissioner, Donna Jones, said England’s south coast was not prepared for the arrival of migrants, and ministers would have a “significant issue” if people traffickers shifted their routes farther west. She warned that places such as Portsmouth were “not set up” for the arrival of migrants.

Kent police defended the action the force took after it described the highly organised protest action in Dover as “spontaneous”. Assistant chief constable Nigel Brookes said the term was used in line with national guidance and that the action had “developed rapidly”.
Eight boats carrying 625 people arrived in the UK on Sunday after crossing the English Channel, Home Office data shows.

articles.title: 3 years on, Morocco earthquake victims still wait for help
articles.summary: Reconstruction has progressed in the three years since the 2023 Morocco earthquake, but some survivors are still living in tents. Locals are divided as to how successful it's been, and whether state…

image.caption: Some locals in the earthquake-hit town of Ighermane in Al Haouz, Morocco — like Mohamed Ait Belaid and his wife — are celebrating a new home after living in a tentImage: Zhor Baki/DW

blocks.text: Reconstruction has progressed in the three years since the 2023 Morocco earthquake, but some survivors are still living in tents. Locals are divided as to how successful it's been, and whether state aid is enough.
On September 8, 2023, a devastating earthquake struck the Al Haouz region in Morocco, killing over 2,900 people, injuring more than 5,500 and causing widespread destruction.

In the village of Ighermane in the High Atlas Mountains, about 50 kilometers (30 miles) southwest of Marrakech, Mohamed Ait Belaid, 72, feels like things are actually going pretty well for him three years later.
He had been living in a tent after the earthquake but now resides in a newly built house, even though it's smaller than the one destroyed in the earthquake.

"I benefited from partial [state] support and received 80,000 dirhams [around €7,300] for rebuilding," he told DW. "I added about 100,000 [€9,110] dirhams from my own pocket. And thanks to God, I like my new house and I'm comfortable in it. I'm at peace because my wife, my children and I are all healthy and I haven't lost any of them."
Around 40 kilometers away, in the town of Azgour, it's a different story. Larbi Ait Jelloulat, also 72, is sitting in front of a pile of rubble that was once his house.

"I want to know where my rights have gone," he said angrily. "Who took what's rightfully mine? For three years, I've been going from one department to another, from one complaint to another, from one petition to another, just looking for an answer. Why have I been excluded? Am I not a Moroccan citizen?"

Ait Jelloulat was formerly a council employee and saved for years in order to build the large home that was destroyed in the 2023 earthquake. As far as he can tell, bureaucratic issues mean he must prove he was a resident in the area.
"My only dream was to spend the rest of my life in my own home, a rest after years of service," he explained. "Now they say I'm not a resident … Where's the logic in that?"

blocks.caption: Larbi Ait Jelloulat sits on the rubble of his home in Azgour; he's been fighting to get state help but has been unsuccessful so far Image: Zhor Baki/DW

blocks.text: Why such different experiences?

Reconstruction seems to be happening faster in Ighermane, the village where Ait Belaid lives. About 90% of the village is rebuilt and most residents' lives are back to normal, said Omar Saeed from the Ighermane Association for Development and Solidarity.
Of the village's around 150 families, 114 received state support of some kind, although most also had to contribute some of their own money to rebuild.
Meanwhile, in Azgour, where Ait Jelloulat lives, there's been more to do. Azgour was the village most impacted by the earthquake in the area.

There, about 76 families have had help with reconstruction, Ait Jelloulat said, while 56 others are still waiting for help. "What's more, the 76 families who rebuilt their homes in a different location are also having problems connecting to water and electricity," he added.

blocks.caption: Azgour village was among those hit hardest by the 2023 earthquake, and reconstruction is still ongoing Image: Zhor Baki/DW

blocks.text: Rebuilding difficult in remote mountain villages

According to a March statement from the High Atlas Development Agency, or ADHA, which was established in October 2023 to bring help to affected areas, 54,425 homes have been built or rehabilitated and more than 3,000 homes are still under construction. The government has given out more than 7.2 billion dirhams (€656 million/$770 million) to affected families. The sum includes funds to help rebuild as well as monthly emergency aid payments.

In terms of the pace of construction, Marrakech-based architect Mohamed Belmejjad believes the state is actually doing fairly well. "I believe the progress so far, relative to the timeframe, to be positive," he told DW.
Given the circumstances, it would be hard for things to have gone much faster, he suggested.
Immediately after the earthquake, it was difficult to reach affected locations, especially remote mountain villages and towns. Then rubble had to be cleared before building could begin.

After that, other factors complicated reconstruction, including the distance of some villages from paved roads, the difficulty of transporting building materials in and debris out, problems with connecting water and power, and the need to relocate whole villages and construction sites to avoid dangers like landslides. There's also a need to respect local building traditions, ensuring that construction materials are solid and will last.

blocks.caption: An injured resident rests near a tent in the shade, holding up her head with her hand

blocks.text: "We also lack the necessary expertise here, whether that's in terms of architects, design offices, contractors or even the labor required for construction," Belmejjad pointed out. Given all that has happened reconstruction could actually be considered ahead of schedule, he suggested.
'No one has remembered us'
Despite that, the National Coordination for Al Haouz Earthquake Victims reports receiving complaints from more than 3,000 families who haven't had any state help.

Montasser Itri, a member of the organization, explains that some of these families were excluded because they had moved to other parts of the country to work and their national identity cards then show them as residents of places unaffected by the 2023 earthquake.

"The government is trying to make us, the victims of the Al Haouz earthquake, into mere statistics linked to the progress of construction and the removal of tents," Itri told DW, "rather than treating us as human beings and with dignity."

blocks.caption: In Amizmiz, local woman Fawzia Aliban is worried her house might collapse before she gets any help Image: Zhor Baki/DW

blocks.text: That's why the coordinating committee is already demanding an independent and transparent investigation into how local authorities have handled the payouts. In the past they've organized demonstrations outside parliament buildings in the capital, Rabat, to demand compensation and rehousing solutions and to accuse local authorities of failing to honor commitments.
Other impacted locals are hoping the upcoming general election, slated for September 23, might make a difference.

"[Prime Minister Aziz] Akhannouch promised us a solution to the issue and God knows we are waiting," said Fawzia Aliban, whose home in Amizmiz was damaged in the earthquake. "We hope the problems will be resolved because I was denied benefits even though my house is on the verge of collapse."

"Three years have passed, and no one has remembered us […] but recently some political figures turned up and promised to solve the problem," added Mohamed Belkaid, who is still living in a tent in the Amizmiz area with his four children.
He hasn't received any aid to rebuild because he is listed as a tenant, not an owner, and is not optimistic things will change.

blocks.caption: Mohamed Belkaid has lived in this tent with his family since the 2023 earthquake Image: Zhor Baki/DW

blocks.text: "They promised to review our files, asking us to trust them and to vote for them," he complained. "But this is exploitation. If they truly wanted to solve the problem, they would have done so before the elections. Where have they been all these years?"
This article was originally written in Arabic.

articles.title: Israeli clearance of Gaza rubble could destroy evidence of 'atrocity crimes,' says UN expert
articles.summary: A U.N. expert said on ‌Monday that Israeli clearance of rubble in Gaza could destroy valuable evidence of "atrocity crimes" and prevent the recovery of human remains.

image.caption: Palestinians walk past the rubble of residential buildings destroyed in Gaza City on Sept. 2. A UN ​expert on the Palestinian territories says evidence should be collected and bodies identified before rubble is cleared. (Dawoud Abu Alkas/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New
A U.N. expert said on ‌Monday that Israeli clearance of rubble in Gaza could destroy valuable evidence of "atrocity crimes" and prevent the recovery of human remains.
UN estimates Gaza has ​61 million tons of rubble; Palestinians say more than 8,000 people buried in debris
A UN expert said on ‌Monday that Israeli clearance of rubble in Gaza could destroy valuable evidence of "atrocity crimes" and prevent the recovery of human remains.

Israel's assault on Gaza — started after the deadly raid into Israel by Hamas in October 2023 — has generated around 61 million tons of wreckage and debris that could take seven ​years to clear, according to the United Nations.

Francesca Albanese, the UN ​expert on the Palestinian territories, issued a statement headlined: "UN expert warns Israeli rubble-clearing could erase traces of atrocity crimes" ​and said Palestinians should be behind any plans to remove waste.

It said her office received information about Israel's "deliberate and widespread removal, crushing and transport of rubble" in August. Albanese said evidence should be gathered and human remains identified before full clearance started.

"In devastated Gaza, rubble is ⁠not just construction waste. It is ⁠part of a crime scene, a graveyard, and ‌the material record of what happened during a brutal and senseless bombing campaign that lasted two years,” she said in the release.

She said that multiple sources had confirmed Israeli companies were involved in the clearance, without naming those sources. Her office did not immediately respond to questions from Reuters on where that information had come from.

Israel's Foreign ⁠Ministry, its prime minister's office and military did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In the past, all have fiercely disagreed with Albanese, who has emerged as one of the most vocal critics of Israel's military actions in Gaza.
In ‌February, Germany, France and Italy all condemned what they said were her overly negative statements about Israel, though she denied making the remarks they cited.

items: They own 2 excavators in Gaza and can't keep up with demand as families dig for remains
Israel prepared to remove Palestinians from Gaza if U.S. approves, defence minister says

blocks.text: In July last year, the U.S. imposed sanctions on Albanese over what it said were her efforts to prompt the International Criminal Court to take action against U.S. ​and Israeli officials, companies and executives.
UN experts are commissioned by the Geneva-based Human Rights Council to monitor and document specific human rights crises but are independent ⁠of the organization itself.
The 2023 Hamas-led attacks killed 1,200 people in Israel while another 251 were taken hostage, according ⁠to Israeli tallies.
More than 73,000 Palestinians have been killed in Israel's military campaign, according to Gaza health authorities.
Israel says ⁠it ⁠has gone to great lengths to avoid ​civilian casualties and that Hamas uses Gaza's civilians as human shields in densely populated areas — a claim Hamas denies.
This family runs 2 of about a dozen remaining excavators in Gaza

In a statement, ​Hamas said it appreciated Albanese's warning, and ⁠urged that the rubble be removed in a manner that "ensures the recovery of the remains of missing persons and the preservation of evidence."

Palestinian authorities estimate more than 8,000 people remain buried in the wreckage. A Palestinian recovery team that combed through the wreckage in Gaza City last month said it found the remains of 112 people from the same clan.

articles.title: UK set to adopt tougher stance on Israel with illegal settlements trade ban
articles.summary:
Ed Miliband to reassert support for Palestinian rights and a two-state solution in move likely to draw fierce criticism from US and Israel

Ed Miliband will announce what he has described as…

blocks.text: Ed Miliband will announce what he has described as a broad reset of the UK’s relations with Israel on Tuesday, promising the government will take a more active approach in supporting the Palestinian cause.

In an intervention that is expected to draw fierce criticism from the US and Israel, the foreign secretary will impose a UK ban on the trade in goods and some services from illegal Israeli settlements. He has also told civil society groups he is determined to reassert the call for a two-state solution to the conflict with an appeal for the protection of Palestinian rights and respect for international law.
In his statement to MPs, Miliband is expected to use firmer language than his recent predecessors in calling out the humanitarian injustices facing Palestinians in Gaza.

The steps he lays out are likely to fall short of the full set of demands made by Palestinian advocacy groups, but they will still be seen as a sign that the UK is moving beyond traditional rhetorical support for a two-state solution towards active steps to forestall the expansion of illegal settlements in the West Bank – widely seen as intended to destroy the prospect of a Palestinian state.

blocks.caption: A Palestinian woman waits at a bus stop decked out with Israeli flags raised by settlers between Nablus and Ramallah in the occupied West Bank. Photograph: Ammar Awad/Reuters

blocks.text: Israel has already threatened reprisals over Miliband’s previous claim that the Israeli military has held back aid into Gaza, and the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, has claimed the Labour government is gripped by Jew hatred. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, spoke to Donald Trump and key Gulf allies such as Qatar on Monday to brief them on his plans in the region.

Miliband’s intervention comes as polling released to the Guardian shows Britons across the political divide strongly favour banning trade with illegal Israeli settlements by a margin of more than two to one.

The polling, conducted by Opinium and published by the European Council on Foreign Relations, shows that only 18% of UK adults oppose a ban on trade in goods with Israeli settlements, compared with 46% in favour. Support rises to nearly three-quarters when those who did not express an opinion are excluded.

Miliband’s statement will stand by his claim that the Israel Defense Forces, in the name of security, are placing unnecessary controls on aid entering Gaza, creating a horrific situation. It is understood, however, that he is sceptical of the UK’s leverage to resolve the situation apart from calling for the restrictions are lifted.

blocks.caption: A Palestinian woman and her children make their way through a destroyed neighbourhood of Gaza City.  Photograph: Mahmoud Issa/Reuters

blocks.text: His claim that aid had been held back was hotly denied by the Israeli foreign ministry at the weekend.

Miliband is also likely to go further than his predecessors in placing the settlement measures firmly in the context of upholding international law, including the findings of its key institutions, the international criminal court and the international court of justice (ICJ), two bodies under attack by the US.

The package is not likely to include sanctions over aid restrictions into Gaza, or to describe what has happened in the territory as a genocide. The UK has kept open the option of joining countries such as South Africa at the ICJ to claim Israel is in breach of the court’s previous rulings.

But by acting decisively on trade, Miliband has set aside warnings that a polarising UK intervention might help Benjamin Netanyahu’s chances in Israel’s 27 October election. British sources pointed out that even Israeli military officials have warned their prime minister that the IDF will struggle to defend new settlements and outposts in the northern West Bank, because they lack basic security infrastructure and were established for political rather than security reasons.

Despite US criticism of the UK stance, Washington has also been putting pressure on Netanyahu on the settlements issue to the point that he has called for some to be dismantled saying they were not established with the necessary permits. Israel has previously demolished some outposts, but they are often rebuilt soon after.

The UK ban on trade in settlement goods, long parried by the Foreign Office as impossible to implement, is in line with the ICJ advisory opinion in 2024 requiring governments not to aid or assist an Israeli occupation of Palestinian territory, not just illegal settlements. The UK government has never formally replied to the opinion, but ministers in Sir Keir Starmer’s administration said it was broadly compliant.

The measures on settlements may require primary legislation to ban the trade in goods rather than an easier statutory instrument, while the trade ban will extend to some services including financing and and advertising illegal settlements.
after newsletter promotion

The Foreign Office has previously argued that it was impossible to distinguish between products emanating from illegal settlements and those from Israel. The UK officially regards all Israeli civilian settlements built on territories captured by during the 1967 six-day war as illegal under international law.
Total trade in goods and services between the UK and Israel in 2025 was £6bn, and the scale of the disruption may depend on Israeli reprisals.

Products produced in Israeli settlements located within the territories occupied by Israel since 1967 have not been entitled to preferential tariff treatment upon entry into the UK since 2005. The country has also issued guidance on misleading labelling and urged businesses not to trade with or be engaged in economic and financial activities in Israeli settlements. The new measures make such investments unlawful.

The UK reset was made more urgent by Israel’s E1 settlement project east of Jerusalem that is poised to effectively cut the occupied West Bank in two from November. But the Burnham government also feels compelled to act because of the increase in settler violence in the West Bank and the failure of Trump’s Board of Peace after six months to secure the twin objectives of Hamas’s disarmament and Israel’s withdrawal from Gaza.

blocks.caption: Israel’s finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, holds up a map showing the E1 settlement project. Photograph: Ohad Zwigenberg/AP

blocks.text: Labour is also under domestic pressure from the Greens on Palestine. The party leader, Zack Polanski, is expected to stand in the 8 October Holborn and St Pancras byelection triggered by Starmer’s resignation as an MP. The new Labour policy may give the party’s candidate some political cover against Polanski.
In a sign of the potential ramifications for Miliband, Netanyahu’s older son, Yair, suggested last week that the Falkland Islands belonged to Argentina and not to Britain.
He is not a minister, but after his comments Trump indicated that Washington could reconsider its position on British sovereignty over the islands.

Trump said last Thursday that he would not back Britain if Argentina were to invade islands, telling GB News: “Your country was not there to help me” when the US and Israel began their war on Iran in February.

articles.title: House probe sought over Visayas power woes
articles.summary: BACOLOD CITY, NEGROS OCCIDENTAL, Philippines — Rotational brownouts lasting as long as nine hours in parts of the Visayas have prompted a move to seek a congressional investigation into the region’s…

blocks.text: BACOLOD CITY, NEGROS OCCIDENTAL, Philippines — Rotational brownouts lasting as long as nine hours in parts of the Visayas have prompted a move to seek a congressional investigation into the region’s worsening power supply crisis.

Deputy House Speaker and Bacolod Rep. Alfredo Abelardo Benitez said the prolonged outages were causing economic losses, disrupting schools, putting medical patients at risk and undermining investor confidence.

“Frequent rotational brownouts in the Visayas region have increased from around one hour to five to nine hours,” Benitez said in a resolution seeking an investigation by the House Committee on Visayas Development.
The inquiry aims to determine accountability among stakeholders and ensure a stable and reliable power supply in the region.
Benitez said the chronic outages could violate consumer protections under the Electric Power Industry Reform Act of 2001 (EPIRA) and the Magna Carta for Residential Electricity Consumers.

As of Sept. 3, the Visayas grid had recorded 93 yellow alerts and 30 red alerts since the start of the year, he said. On Sept. 4, the National Grid Corporation of the Philippines (NGCP) issued another yellow and red alert due to severe supply shortages.

An NGCP report identified Cebu as the grid’s weak link, citing a simulated evening peak shortfall of 422 megawatts (MW). Peak demand reached 1,077 MW against dependable capacity of only 655 MW, forcing load shedding and requiring power transfers from Panay, Negros, Leyte-Samar and Bohol, Benitez said.

The report also showed that 12 power plants in the region suffered forced outages in September alone. Another 17 generating units had remained offline for extended periods, including three since 2025, two since 2024, two since 2023 and one since 2021.
With 16 other plants operating at reduced capacity, a total of 972.6 MW had become unavailable to the grid, he said.

Benitez cited the unavailability of major coal plants, including Toledo Power Inc. Unit 1 and Panay Energy Development Corp. Unit 3; tripping incidents along the Leyte-A (Maha) transmission lines and at Cebu Energy Development Corp. Unit 1; outages at Panay Diesel Power Plant Units 3-E and 3-H and Central Negros Power Reliability Inc. Unit 2; and limited power imports from Mindanao.

He questioned whether generation companies and grid operators were complying with maintenance standards, rehabilitation obligations and license requirements, given that the outages had persisted for years.
Benitez urged the Energy Regulatory Commission to strictly enforce performance standards, review power supply agreements and promote greater transparency in electricity pricing and fuel procurement.
The proposed inquiry will also examine energy mix options that could help lower electricity costs.

Benitez asked the committee to invite officials from the NGCP, Department of Energy, ERC, power generation companies, electric cooperatives, distribution utilities, and other affected stakeholders to explain their immediate measures to address the power shortages. /cb

articles.title: German chancellor vows to stay in office despite AfD triumph in state election
articles.summary:
Friedrich Merz said his conservative CDU was shaken ‘to its very foundations’ after far-right victory in Saxony-Anhalt

A “shocked” and chastened Friedrich Merz has vowed to stay in office…

blocks.text: A “shocked” and chastened Friedrich Merz has vowed to stay in office despite the far right’s triumph in a state election that has brought anti-immigrant, pro-Kremlin politicians within striking distance of power.

The German chancellor, appearing ashen-faced in front of reporters in Berlin, said on Monday that the landslide victory by the Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) in Saxony-Anhalt had shaken his conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) “to its very foundations”.

The unpopular Merz, who had pledged to halve the AfD’s support at the national level, has watched the nativist party rack up electoral gains, none as convincing as its utter rout of the CDU in the eastern region on Sunday with nearly 44% of the vote.
The AfD and its candidate Ulrich Siegmund fell short of an absolute majority but could yet create Germany’s first far-right state government since the Nazi period.

Merz appeared contrite and willing to work on his “communication” with voters. “This is the worst electoral defeat the [CDU] has suffered in years, in decades,” he said. “Of course this will have to have consequences.”

Exit polls indicated the state’s voters were driven by deep dissatisfaction with the political establishment and its stewardship of Europe’s biggest economy, with one showing that only 9% approved of Merz’s performance.

blocks.caption: Ulrich Siegmund mocked Merz as ‘a very good campaigner’ for the AfD.  Photograph: Odd Andersen/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Siegmund, a media-savvy former fragrance salesman, was also able to tap into a sense of grievance in the former communist east, where complaints abound that voters there are treated as “second-class citizens” more than three decades after the fall of the Berlin Wall.
Siegmund, 35, mocked the 70-year-old Merz as “a very good campaigner” for the AfD.

Only 16 months in office, Merz conceded his own low poll ratings had played a role in his party’s loss. “I know that I personally was a constant topic in this election campaign,” he said. “We must try – myself included – to reach people more effectively, in the full range of their emotions.”
The CDU’s junior coalition partner, the Social Democrats, indicated a willingness to water down contentious measures to shore up the statutory healthcare and pension schemes.

However, Merz insisted: “My determination to continue on the path of reform is unbroken,” saying a sustainable system was essential for the sake of “our children and grandchildren”. He added: “Giving up is not an option for me.”

Merz said he wanted to assure Germany’s allies that “our institutions are resilient and stable” and its own vulnerable minorities that the country would stick to its values and constitution even if the AfD took power in Saxony-Anhalt. “We know that Germany carries special responsibility because of its history,” he said.
He also promised to stay the course on Ukraine, stressing he would “not budge a single millimetre from my fundamental conviction that we must defend our freedom against Russia as well”.

Merz said Moscow would cheer the AfD’s success in Saxony-Anhalt and accused it of lending support to the far right’s campaign, with another two German state elections still to come this month amid alleged Russian interference and sabotage.

blocks.caption: Sven Schulze, the CDU state premier for Saxony-Anhalt, acknowledged his party now had ‘no mandate’ to govern in the state. Photograph: Annegret Hilse/Reuters

blocks.text: Although the CDU rallied behind its chancellor and party leader, several influential commenters openly called for his immediate replacement – a complex step under German law.
after newsletter promotion

Germany “needs a clean slate, a fresh start, and that starts with Friedrich Merz”, said the Der Spiegel editor-in-chief, Dirk Kurbjuweit. “He is evidently the wrong man for this office in these times.”

The AfD’s Saxony-Anhalt chapter is listed as “confirmed rightwing extremist” by the domestic intelligence service. It has pledged mass deportations of unwelcome immigrants and asylum seekers, which critics have said would be illegal, while promising massive boosts in social welfare spending with unclear financing.
The AfD has also taken aim at state support for public broadcasters and cultural institutions it deems “unpatriotic”, sparking fears of “cultural hegemony”.

The party did not win enough seats to elect Siegmund as state premier, but AfD leaders said they seek to pick off rebel lawmakers from other parties willing to play kingmaker. It is only three seats short of a majority.

The conservative-left populist BSW party, which also favours restoring ties with Russia and largely blocking immigration, signalled an openness to working with the AfD but before the election ruled out joining the state government.

In the 13 years of the AfD’s existence, the mainstream parties have maintained a “firewall” against the far right, refusing any formal cooperation that would allow it take power. The strategy meant to sideline the party has appeared to backfire, however, as the permanent “outsider” role appeals to legions of voters fed up with politics as usual.

The CDU state premier, Sven Schulze, acknowledged his party had “no mandate” to govern given its humiliating 17% result, even if it managed to cobble together an unwieldy coalition with all the other parties in the legislature.

Although Saxony-Anhalt forms part of the AfD heartland as a relatively poor, ex-communist region, the party has begun making inroads in the west as well amid alarming signs of decline in the steel, chemicals and automotive sectors.
Germany faces another two regional elections on 20 September, in Berlin and in another eastern state, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, where the AfD is also strong.
The party co-leader Alice Weidel, beaming after Sunday’s vote, said the AfD was now targeting 40% at the next general election, due in 2029. It is polling at about 28%.
