articles.title: EU's Von der Leyen pledges $232 million Greenland investment
articles.summary: The EU is preparing a major investment package and closer political ties with the Danish Arctic territory amid Donald Trump's demand for greater US control of the mineral-rich island.

image.caption: Von der Leyen (right) said the visit was about further cementing a unique partnership with the regionImage: Mads Claus Rasmussen/Ritzau Scanpix/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has pledged €200 million ($232 million) investment package for Greenland as the EU seeks closer relations with the Arctic territory.

Von der Leyen has been visiting Nuuk, the capital of thje Danish autonomous island, for the past two days where she met with Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenlandic counterpart Jens-Frederik Nielsen.
Von der Leyen's visit comes after threats of US annexation earlier this year by President Donald Trump.
What von der Leyen said?
"Territorial integrity sovereignty, the inviolability of borders, these are fundamental principles of international law," von der Leyen told a joint press conference.
The EU chief announced the "EU-Greenland Partnership Package," focusing on three priorities: connectivity, clean energy and critical raw materials.
"This is 200 million euros of new investments for Greenland for this year and the next," von der Leyen said.
She emphasized that "Greenland's future is for the people of Greenland and Denmark to decide, no one else."
The European Commission head arrived in Nuuk on Sunday in a show of support for Greenland and Denmark, and was received by Nielsen and Frederiksen.

"We’re deepening our cooperation across the board. Connectivity, clean energy, critical raw materials. And of course, more opportunities for the people of Greenland," Von der Leyen said in a post on X.
What does the EU investment package include?
The EU package is expected to include hundreds of millions of euros in investment in:

items: critical minerals
satellite communications
renewable energy

blocks.text: Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen described the visit as an opportunity to deepen the territory's "close friendship and good partnership" with the EU.
The largely autonomous Greenland left the EU in 1985, although its population of about 57,000 are EU citizens through Danish citizenship.
Why is Trump demanding 'total access' over Greenland?

Von der Leyen's visit comes as the Arctic gains strategic importance for the US, Russia, China and Europe, with melting sea ice opening new shipping routes and increasing access to the region's mineral resources.

Trump has repeatedly stated that the US "needs" Greenland for its "national security," pointing to his claims — without providing evidence — that the island is "covered with Chinese and Russian ships all over the place."
Trump has maintained that Denmark cannot adequately defend the island against China and Russia.

His campaign bid to gain "total access" to the Danish territory has strained US-European relations and raised tensions within NATO as both Greenland and the Danish government have rejected Trump's demands.
Greenland's ice-covered minerals: No easy option

articles.title: Loren Legarda praises enactment of stronger free college law
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — More students from poor families can now stay in school and finish their education, Sen. Loren Legarda said as she welcomed on Monday the enactment of Republic Act No. 12325,…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — More students from poor families can now stay in school and finish their education, Sen. Loren Legarda said as she welcomed on Monday the enactment of Republic Act No. 12325, which strengthens the Universal Access to Quality Tertiary Education.

The new law, signed by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Sept. 4, improves the tertiary education subsidy (TES) by directing assistance more deliberately toward the poorest students and recognizing that the cost of education goes far beyond tuition.

“It’s not enough that tuition is free if students have no money for fare to go to school and buy books, and then are short of money to buy food, or are forced to stop to help their families. Free college must mean that a student has a real chance not only to enroll, but to stay in school and graduate,” Legarda said in a mix of Filipino and English in a statement issued on Monday.
More focus on poor students

Legarda principally sponsored and authored Senate Bill No. 1894, which strengthened Republic Act No. 10931 by making student assistance more responsive to the actual financial burden of pursuing college or technical-vocational education.

Among its key reforms is focusing the subsidy more on students who need government assistance most, particularly senior high school graduates from Pantawid Pamilyang Pilipino Program (4Ps) households who are admitted to qualified higher education or technical-vocational institutions.

The reform addresses a significant gap identified by the Second Congressional Commission on Education (Edcom II). Legarda now serves as an Edcom II commissioner, previously serving as its co-chairperson. She was also the chairperson of the Senate Committee on Higher, Technical, and Vocational Education

As Legarda points out, the share of TES beneficiaries from the poorest households fell from 70.73 percent in 2018 to 22.89 percent in 2022. Of 384,388 senior high school graduates from 4Ps households, only 4,746, or 1.23 percent, received TES as first-year beneficiaries in academic year 2024–2025.

“The data is clear. Many youths who should get aid first don’t benefit from it. We strengthened the system to make sure that more families in need will get the opportunity to let their children finish. We can’t describe an opportunity as universal if the poorest are the ones who get aid last,” Legarda said.
Regular subsidy reviews
The new law also provides for regular reviews of TES amounts so that it can respond to changes in the actual cost of education.

To make tertiary education more inclusive, state universities and colleges, local universities and colleges, and state-run technical-vocational institutions are also required to adopt Equity and Inclusion Plans.
This aims to remove barriers faced by persons with disabilities, students from geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas, indigenous peoples, and learners from other disadvantaged backgrounds.

The law also establishes the Private Education Assistance Program, which will support qualified students who need financial assistance in private higher education institutions and technical-vocational schools.

Legarda pointed out that the law advances a principle she had been consistently pushing in education policy — that government must look beyond how many students enter school and focus on whether they are actually able to finish.

“We hope to ensure that no Filipino youth will lose the opportunity to get a quality education just because their families lack money. The lack of money should not be a reason for their education to be cut short and their dreams blocked,” she said. /atm

articles.title: Ilocos Sur town probes dredging near its waters
articles.summary: SAN ILDEFONSO, Ilocos Sur — The municipal government of Sta. Lucia said it would not tolerate unauthorized or environmentally harmful dredging within its jurisdiction, citing the need to protect…

blocks.text: SAN ILDEFONSO, Ilocos Sur — The municipal government of Sta. Lucia said it would not tolerate unauthorized or environmentally harmful dredging within its jurisdiction, citing the need to protect marine ecosystems and the livelihoods of coastal communities.

The statement came after municipal officials inspected a dredging activity off Barangay Nangalisan on Monday, Sept. 7, to determine whether the operation falls within Sta. Lucia’s territorial waters and assess its possible environmental impact.
The initial on-site assessment showed that the dredging site was about 1,933 meters from the identified municipal boundary toward Sabangan, an area under neighboring Sta. Cruz town.

Mayor Joseph Simon Valdez, Vice Mayor Eduardo Toquero, members of the Sangguniang Bayan, barangay officials and representatives from the Municipal Engineering and Assessor’s offices joined the inspection, along with personnel from the police and Bureau of Fire Protection.

The local government said the measurement and site inspection form part of its continuing verification of the dredging operation’s exact location in relation to the boundaries of Sta. Lucia and Sta. Cruz.
Officials also documented conditions in the area and assessed the possible effects of the dredging on the coastal environment.
The municipal government said it would coordinate with concerned government agencies to determine whether the operation complies with environmental laws and other regulations. /mcm

articles.title: Eastern Visayas power coops warn of outages amid grid alert
articles.summary: TACLOBAN CITY — Electric cooperatives in Eastern Visayas warned consumers Monday, Sept. 7, of possible power interruptions as the National Grid Corporation of the Philippines (NGCP) placed the…

blocks.text: TACLOBAN CITY — Electric cooperatives in Eastern Visayas warned consumers Monday, Sept. 7, of possible power interruptions as the National Grid Corporation of the Philippines (NGCP) placed the Visayas grid under red and yellow alerts due to tight power supply.
NGCP said it may implement Manual Load Dropping (MLD) from 4 p.m. to 9 p.m. in areas served by the following distribution utilities and electric cooperatives:

items: Leyte Electric Cooperative II (Leyeco II)
Southern Leyte Electric Cooperative (Soleco)
Don Orestes Romualdez Electric Cooperative Inc. (Dorelco)
Leyeco III
Leyeco IV
Leyeco V
Eastern Samar Electric Cooperative (Esamelco)
Biliran Electric Cooperative (Bileco)
Northern Samar Electric Cooperative (Norsamelco)
Samar I Electric Cooperative (Samelco I)
Samar II Electric Cooperative (Samelco II)

blocks.text: About one million member-consumers are served by these distribution utilities across the region.
The possible power interruptions are intended to help protect the stability of the power grid amid limited generation and power imports from Mindanao, NGCP said.
The Visayas grid was placed under red alert from 6 p.m. to 7 p.m. and yellow alert from 3 p.m. to 6 p.m. and 7 p.m. to 9 p.m.
NGCP reported available capacity of 2,530 megawatts (MW) against a projected peak demand of 2,508 MW, leaving only a slim reserve.

It attributed the tight supply situation to the unavailability of the large coal-fired plants TVI 1 and PEDC 3, the 146.2-MW derating of THVI 2 due to a main steam problem, and limited power imports from Mindanao.
Eight power plants were on forced outage, while 15 others were operating at reduced capacity, resulting in a total of 818.9 MW of unavailable capacity.
NGCP said the MLD schedule may still be canceled if system conditions improve, such as when actual electricity demand falls below projections.

A red alert means available supply is insufficient to meet demand and the grid’s regulating requirement, while a yellow alert indicates that the operating margin is insufficient to meet the grid’s contingency requirement.
NGCP urged consumers to use electricity prudently, particularly during peak hours. /mcm

articles.title: Manila Water eyes completing San Juan Reservoir by end of 2026
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — As climate-related challenges and natural hazards become more frequent and severe, Manila Water is strengthening the resilience of its water supply infrastructure through the…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — As climate-related challenges and natural hazards become more frequent and severe, Manila Water is strengthening the resilience of its water supply infrastructure through the ongoing construction of the new San Juan Reservoir, a critical facility designed to withstand major earthquakes and support reliable water service for decades to come.

Targeted for completion by the end of 2026, the new 56-million-liter (ML) reservoir will replace the existing San Juan Reservoir and serve as a more robust and resilient water storage facility for communities in Metro Manila. Designed in accordance with modern engineering standards, the new reservoir incorporates upgraded structural, electrical, instrumentation, and mechanical systems that will help ensure uninterrupted service even in the face of increasing environmental and seismic risks.

The project forms part of Manila Water’s continuing investments to modernize and future-proof its water infrastructure amid growing challenges posed by urbanization, extreme weather events, and natural disasters.
The replacement project was pursued following extensive structural assessments of the existing San Juan Reservoir, which was originally constructed in 1968.

Engineering studies conducted by DCCD Engineering Corporation in 2011 and 2016 identified significant deterioration in the facility’s roof slab and walls resulting from decades of service. The assessments also indicated a high risk of structural failure during major seismic events, including a potential 7.2-magnitude earthquake.

In addition, the reservoir’s top slab had undergone several repairs due to holes and other defects that could potentially compromise the quality and safety of stored water supplying the San Juan Pumping Station.
Recognizing the need to enhance the long-term reliability and disaster resilience of the facility, Manila Water moved forward with the replacement of the aging reservoir.

With a total project cost of more than ₱970 million, the undertaking covers the demolition of the existing reservoir and the design and construction of the new 56-ML facility, including all associated electrical, instrumentation, mechanical, and site development works.
As of July 2026, construction progress has reached 84 percent, with work continuing toward the project’s targeted completion by the end of the year.

Once operational, the new San Juan Reservoir will strengthen the reliability of water supply service while providing greater resilience against earthquakes and other hazards that could affect critical water infrastructure.

“By investing in more resilient facilities, such as the San Juan Reservoir, we are enhancing our ability to continue delivering safe, reliable, and uninterrupted water service to the communities we serve, even during disruptive events,” Manila Water Corporate Communications Group Head Dittie Galang said.

The new San Juan Reservoir underscores Manila Water’s commitment to building infrastructure that not only meets growing water demand but also strengthens the resilience of the East Zone’s water supply system in an increasingly hazard-prone environment.

articles.title: P48.9M ‘smuggled’ cigarettes seized in Pampanga, 4 men arrested
articles.summary: MABALACAT CITY — The police arrested four men for transporting some an estimated P48,955,500 worth of suspected smuggled cigarettes in Barangay Cacutud here shortly after midnight on Monday. In a…

blocks.text: MABALACAT CITY — The police arrested four men for transporting some an estimated P48,955,500 worth of suspected smuggled cigarettes in Barangay Cacutud here shortly after midnight on Monday.
In a statement, the Police Regional Office 3 (PRO3) said the operation which resulted in the arrest was carried out after several days of surveillance operations.
Authorities had received information that a truck was being used to transport and store cases of suspected illicit cigarettes at a secluded location in the city.

At around 12:30 a.m., operatives from the Regional Special Operations Group-Regional Intelligence Division 3, Mabalacat City Police Station, and Criminal Investigation and Detection Group Regional Field Unit 3 successfully intercepted the target truck and arrested its driver and three companions.

“A search of the truck led to the discovery of 759 master cases of ‘Modern’ cigarettes — 329 master cases of red packs and 430 master cases of blue packs. The products were observed to have no Bureau of Internal Revenue tax stamps and remain subject to further examination and verification,” the PRO3 said.

PRO3 Director Brig. Gen. Jess Mendez said the impact of the operation went beyond the amount of contraband seized, noting that illicit trade deprives the government of potential revenues that could support public services, puts legitimate businesses at a disadvantage, and allows illegal trade networks to profit at the expense of lawful commerce.
“Keeping these products off the market helps protect consumers, businesses, and the local economy,” he added.
The PRO3 said the recovered items were inventoried in the presence of the arrested individuals and a barangay official.
Alternative recording devices were also used during the operation in accordance with existing procedures.
The four arrested individuals and the recovered evidence were brought to the police regional camp for documentation and proper disposition.

According to PRO3, it was coordinating with the appropriate government agencies to determine the applicable violations to be filed against the arrested persons and to conduct further examination and verification of the recovered cigarette products. /gsg

articles.title: Threatening letters revive fears among Kashmiri Pandits
articles.summary: Leaked addresses and phone numbers have reignited fears among Hindu government employees who returned to Muslim-majority Kashmir under a rehabilitation scheme.

image.caption: Kashmiri Hindus, known locally as Pandits, have long complained of a lack of security [FILE: June 2022]Image: Channi Anand/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: A new wave of threatening letters targeting Kashmiri Pandits — members of the Hindu minority community who fled the Muslim-majority Kashmir Valley during a militant uprising in the 1990s — has deepened fears among those who have returned to the region as civil servants under an Indian government federal rehabilitation scheme.
The latest letters, which surfaced in the last week of August, named several employees. The letters also included their Jammu residential addresses, vehicle registration numbers and phone numbers.
Personal details exposed

"Similar threat letters surfaced in early August, but the latest contains our Jammu residential address, vehicle and phone numbers, which have also been shared on social media," Anil Koul, a government employee, told DW, urging authorities to investigate the source of the leak.

The letters have been attributed to a little-known group calling itself the United Liberation Council, which security officials suspect could be a front for the Pakistan-based Islamist militant outfit Lashkar-e-Taiba.

The group reportedly first surfaced in July, when it released a poster marking the death anniversary of a former militant commander. Authorities have yet to confirm the letters' authenticity or the existence of the group behind them.

The latest letters also distinguish between Pandits who never left the Valley — and are therefore "safe" — and those recruited under New Delhi's rehabilitation program, who are accused of working for "masters" outside Kashmir.
The fresh threats have also triggered a political row.

Jammu and Kashmir National Conference (JKNC) president and former Jammu and Kashmir chief minister, Farooq Abdullah, called them a "conspiracy" aimed at delaying the restoration of statehood, which the region lost in 2019.
Abdullah also questioned why Hindu officers from outside the region were not facing similar threats.
His remarks drew sharp criticism from Kashmiri Pandit groups and the ruling Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which accused him of being insensitive to the community's fears.
Familiar fears
Government records show 44,167 Kashmiri migrant families registered as having left since 1990 citing security concerns, of which 39,782 were Hindu.
For Pandit community representatives, however, the latest threats are part of a much longer security problem.

Sanjay Tickoo, president of the Kashmiri Pandit Struggle Committee (KPSS), said the threats should be viewed against the backdrop of targeted killings and repeated security concerns faced by Pandit government employees in the Valley. He blames security lapses and says repeated meetings with officials since a wave of killings in 2022 have failed to resolve their concerns.
"Since 2022, meetings have resulted in nothing," Tickoo told DW. He also wondered how those making the threats have access to employees' personal details.
"How are these details being posted on social media?" Tickoo asked.
Targeted killings have occurred sporadically in the years since. At least seven Kashmiri Pandits were killed by militants during a spike in violence between 2020 and 2022.
One of the starkest cases was that of Rahul Bhat, a Pandit revenue official who was shot dead inside his government office in Budgam in May 2022.
The last confirmed targeted killing of a Kashmiri Pandit was in October 2022, when Puran Krishan Bhat, an orchard farmer, was shot dead in Shopian district.
Former Jammu and Kashmir police chief S P Vaid described the latest threats as part of a familiar militant playbook.
"There is nothing new in this," Vaid told DW, calling it "a ploy by Pakistan to Islamize society." He said similar tactics had been used against migrant workers in the Valley.

The difference, this time, is the precision of the threats. Personal data that should not have been so easily accessible has been made public, and no clear explanation of how it was leaked has been provided.
Kashmir: Fears dampen celebrations at Hindu festival
The return dilemma

The KPSS estimates roughly 6,500 Pandits who never left the Valley, along with another 4,000 who have returned as government employees under a federal rehabilitation scheme, live in India-administered Kashmir.
But the reintegration of those who fled decades ago has proved challenging.
Rahul Pandita, a journalist and author of "Our Moon Has Blood Clots: A Memoir of a Lost Home in Kashmir," said the government's record on rehabilitation was inadequate.

"The BJP has had no rehabilitation policy for Kashmiri Hindus," Pandita told DW, arguing that the government employees in the Valley had returned under a policy introduced during the previous government of former Prime Minister Manmohan Singh.
Some land has been returned and cases of killings investigated, he said, but "it is too little and too late."
Pandita said the bigger problem was that no government could guarantee a completely secure environment for a mass return.

"No matter what the government does, the situation will never be conducive enough for the Pandits to return," he said, arguing that as long as Islamist militancy exists in the region, Kashmiri Hindus would still be targeted.
"It's for them then to decide if they are willing to take such a risk," he said.
Beyond government employees, some Pandits who have returned and established businesses in the Valley are already living there quietly, Pandita said.
"That is the best-case scenario for Kashmiri Pandits in Kashmir Valley," he said.

blocks.caption: Pandits accuse the government in New Delhi of not doing enough to protect them from alleged Islamist threatsImage: Firdous Nazir/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Security beyond protection
Sushobha Barve, executive secretary of the Center for Dialogue and Reconciliation, said the latest threats expose a wider security paradox.
"Despite claims of normalcy, a tiny group of active militants has successfully disrupted the lives of migrant families. Breaking the cycle of panic is essential," Barve told DW.
She said there was also growing political frustration over the delay in restoring Jammu and Kashmir's statehood, arguing that this grievance cut across the region.

Amitabh Mattoo, an academic and professor of international relations at Jawaharlal Nehru University who has written extensively on Kashmir, said any return of Kashmiri Pandits had to be both secure and dignified.

"The state has an essential role in ensuring their physical security and in protecting their property, cultural and other legitimate rights. But security measures alone will not suffice," Mattoo told DW.
"A sustainable return will also require patient reconciliation, engagement with local civil society, and the gradual rebuilding of inter-community trust and social and economic ties."
How India reshaped Kashmir by revoking Article 370

articles.title: Legal veterans lead fightback against Trump’s ‘full-out assault on democracy’
articles.summary:
Advocacy groups expand legal challenges and condemn president’s ‘self-serving attempts to take over midterms’

A cluster of advocacy groups that boast veteran lawyers, voting experts and…

blocks.text: A cluster of advocacy groups that boast veteran lawyers, voting experts and ex-judges have expanded legal challenges to Donald Trump’s authoritarian executive orders on voting and other presidential actions they see as a “war” on the rule of law in the US.

Heavy legal opposition to Trump’s two executive orders on elections to curb voting rights and supplant the authority of states on election matters has come from the Democracy Defenders Fund, the Campaign Legal Center, the American Civil Liberties Union and kindred groups.

These legal outfits and like-minded allies have won key lawsuits on election issues, plus litigation thwarting Trump’s moves to end birthright citizenship and a $1.8bn slush fund that could have paid money to allies including January 6 rioters he deemed were unjustly charged.

Since Trump returned to power, for instance, Democracy Defenders Fund and the Campaign Legal Center have jointly filed lawsuits against Trump’s 2025 and 2026 executive orders on voting, challenging their constitutionality to set new voting rules that by law are run by the states.

Key legal briefs they filed together include an August one on behalf of several voting rights groups and local officials in two states to block Trump’s March 2026 executive order that would restrict voting by mail and authorize the US Postal Service to implement rules to that end.

Other groups that have accelerated their legal challenges to Trump’s moves to thwart voting rights and expand his executive powers in other ways, include the Brennan Center for Justice, Democracy Forward, the Democratic Attorneys General Association and the Washington Litigation Group.

Last month, for instance, 24 Democratic attorney generals and other plaintiffs filed suit to block USPS from moving forward with rules to curb mail voting and in late August won a temporary 14-day restraining order from federal judge Indira Talwani in Massachusetts.

In response, the DoJ’s solicitor general John Sauer on Thursday appealed to the supreme court to lift the injunction, arguing in heated words that the freeze would create “serious, irreparable harm on the federal government, the states themselves, and the voting public”.

On 4 September Talwani made her injunction permanent, writing that implementing Trump’s order so close to the election “threatens disenfranchisement of millions of United States citizens who seek to vote by mail.” She also stressed that “the record includes no evidence relating to fraudulent mail voting to support the rushed implementation.”

Sauer on 6 September responded with another emergency appeal to the high court urging it permit the new USPS rules to go into effect, claiming that it “does not seize control of states’ administration of elections — it simply imposes reasonable preparation requirements for certain election-related mail.”

In a related twist, a detailed whistleblower complaint that Democratic senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut released last week alleged that the USPS has been proceeding with a “secretive, rushed” effort to implement Trump’s order that could lead to “catastrophic failure” with this year’s mail-in voting.
About 50 million Americans, the majority of whom are Democrats, vote by mail, according to reports.

With the elections about two months away, the legal groups are stepping up efforts to thwart “self-serving attempts to take over the midterms”, said a former DoJ lawyer, which experts fear may create chaos and disenfranchise millions of voters.

Anna Baldwin, director of voting rights litigation at the Campaign Legal Center, told the Guardian: “The CLC and the DDF have worked closely together on two ongoing lawsuits challenging the president’s unlawful voting executive orders that attempt to dictate election rules. We’ve teamed up in the supreme court on a brief filed by former state and federal judges, including noted conservative judges, that emphasized just how unlawful and dangerous the president’s efforts to dictate election rules are.”

Baldwin, who spent 14 years in the justice department’s civil rights division, said the CLC and the DDF have also “worked together in federal cases filed in Oregon and California to make sure that the DoJ isn’t able to seize voters’ sensitive data by making false claims about non-citizen voting. In cases around the country, the Campaign Legal Center is pushing back on the DoJ’s lawless efforts to vacuum up and aggregate sensitive data to create a national voter file of some sort.”

Further, former ambassador Norm Eisen, the executive chair of the Democracy Defenders Fund, which he co-founded in 2023, told the Guardian that since its inception the DDF has been involved in more than 300 legal cases and matters in three primary areas: elections, the rule of law and anti-corruption.

Eisen said the group, whose board boasts former federal judge and conservative stalwart J Michael Luttig and liberal-leaning ex-federal judge Nancy Gertner, likes to work in conjunction on cases with other ideologically diverse and nonpartisan groups like the CLC and the WLG because “they both have strong bipartisan credibility. It’s a big-tent approach we’ve taken with our election work.”

Eisen said Luttig and Gertner were instrumental in helping recruit dozens of former judges with bipartisan credentials to file amicus briefs on multiple matters including an August one to the supreme court opposing Trump’s 2026 executive order to curb mail voting.

For its part, the WLG this summer hired about half a dozen new lawyers to handle election-related litigation. “As the midterms approach with growing concerns about potential federal interference in elections, we’ve brought on more attorneys to be even more prepared to litigate sensitive matters under acute time pressure,” said James Pearce, a principal with the WLG.

blocks.caption: A Kentucky voter in Louisville casts her ballot. Photograph: Bryan Woolston/Reuters

blocks.text: Elsewhere, Sophia Lin Lakin, who leads the ACLU Voting Rights Project, said the group had been “pushing back” on administration efforts to seize personal voting data from states, and said the ACLU has been involved in 26 of 30 legal challenges to the administration on the issue. To date, the administration has lost 23 cases where rulings have been made.

Critics say Trump, the DoJ, the USPS and the Department of Homeland Security seem to be laying the groundwork for further attacks on the nation’s election rules, citing Trump’s false claims about election fraud and his radical plans to change voting rules.

In July in a televised speech, Trump falsely portrayed the nation’s voting system as riddled with fraud and condemned voting by mail and non-citizen voting. “Mail-in ballots are inherently corrupt,” Trump claimed without evidence, even though he voted twice by mail this year.

Trump, who continues to blame voting fraud for his 2020 loss to Joe Biden, also charged that non-citizen voting, which is illegal and historically minuscule, poses a “crisis of election security”. Trump’s fixation on noncitizen voting is belied by a database from the rightwing Heritage Foundation that only cites 100 cases over a quarter-century.

But according to documents reviewed by the New York Times, hundreds of DHS agents have been engaged in a hunt to find noncitizens among registered voters. The chief of the DHS has said ICE agents could be sent to polling places “if there is a threat to that polling place or we’re serving a warrant”.
The DoJ has helped to amplify Trump’s bogus election claims with legal threats and actions.

In July, Harmeet Dhillon, who runs the department’s civil rights division, wrote to officials in 50 states warning that “any election officer, including the chief election officer of the state, who knowingly retains noncitizens on the state’s [voter list] or facilitates noncitizens in receiving and casting ballots could be subject to criminal liability”.
In August, the DoJ announced plans to send a larger-than-usual contingent of 1,000 lawyers to monitor voting nationwide, raising concerns that such large efforts could lead to voter intimidation.

And in a harbinger of coming legal fights, Trump announced on his Truth Social platform last month that the DoJ’s Ed Martin, a key election denialist in charge of pardons, was leaving to handle election-related litigation.
Former DoJ lawyers say administration threats to voting rights make opposition from legal advocates crucial.

Stacey Young, a lawyer who left the department at the start of 2025 after 18 years to found Justice Connection, a group of more than 3,000 ex-DoJ lawyers and other alumni, denounced Trump’s moves “to interfere” with elections.

“The constitution makes clear that the president has no authority over the administration of our elections, but that hasn’t stopped this president, or those he put in power at the justice department, from trying to interfere,” Young said in a statement. “We’re taking these threats seriously and leveraging our collective strengths to protect election integrity, which is key to maintaining a functioning democracy.”

Justice Connection is working with experts in its alumni network to engage with the media, Congress and the public to highlight the justice department’s traditional role in election security and ensuring compliance with federal voting laws.
Other DoJ alumni agree that opposition to Trump’s election agenda is critical.

“These organizations are doing critical work in protecting the ability of people to vote and make their voices heard – a cornerstone of democracy,” said Michael Bromwich, a former DoJ inspector general. “The full-out assault on democracy must be addressed through the courts because Congress has proven itself unwilling and unable to check the undemocratic steps taken by the administration.”

Barbara McQuade, a former US attorney for eastern Michigan who now teaches law at the University of Michigan, said: “Large law firms sent armies of young attorneys to our nation’s airports to represent individuals caught up in Trump’s travel ban. That is not happening any more because of the ‘deals’ they negotiated with the Trump administration in his second term to support his pet causes.

“Thank goodness for groups like the Democracy Defenders Fund, which are attracting top legal talent and challenging some of Trump’s lawless activities. Their work is protecting the rights of all Americans.”

Further, Nick Brown, Washington state’s attorney general, who chairs an election protection group for the Democratic Attorneys General Association, said it has teamed up with some legal advocacy groups such as the Brennan Center, States United and the DDF to hold “strategy sessions” to prepare for potential disruptive moves by the Trump administration in the November elections.

Brown also attacked the administration’s appeal to the supreme court to move forward with Trump’s executive order on voting by mail, despite Judge Talwani’s strong concerns and Daga’s litigation against it.

He said: “As the court said, states’ compliance with this illegal order would be ‘practically impossible’ before the November elections given the unprecedented demands it would put on state and local elections officials. The chaos that would cause is exactly what Trump wants. That’s why we continue to fight for a fair and properly administered election.”
Baldwin too raised strong concerns about the DoJ’s push to get the supreme court to issue a ruling that would expedite Trump’s executive order on voting by mail.

She said: “The DoJ’s slapdash effort at getting the supreme court’s blessing to turn the USPS into a gatekeeper for mail would be a farce, if it didn’t put our fundamental right to vote in the crosshairs. Given the importance of what is at stake, the DoJ’s continued efforts are nothing more than an attempt to foist chaos on the electoral process. But they will fail.”
Other lawyers engaged in key election legal battles and other litigation voice optimism they will prevail.

Tianna Mays, the legal director of the DDF, said: “The Trump administration has declared war on the rule of law, yet our democratic guardrails are still holding. We refuse to stand by idly while this administration flouts the constitution and attempts to eviscerate our institutions.”

articles.title: Elon Musk thanked by German far-right leader after landmark election win praised by Russia | First Thing
articles.summary: Populist, far-right, anti-immigration AfD wins vote in eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt. Plus, 50 years since The Muppet Show first hit our screens

blocks.text: Good morning. A far-right leader who has won an important state election in Germany has thanked Elon Musk for his support, as voices in Europe warn the result is a serious moment for the continent. No far-right party has led or formed a government in Germany since the defeat of nazism at the end of the second world war.

Ulrich Siegmund, the Alternative für Deutschland’s lead candidate, thanked Musk on X after the tech billionaire said “Well done!” in German to the AfD co-founder Alice Weidel. The populist, far-right, anti-immigration party won the vote in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.

During its campaign, the AfD sought to capitalise on a mood of nostalgia for the communist East Germany and discontent among east Germans. The party has promised a remigration and deportation offensive, to ban rainbow flags in schools and halt the building of new windfarms. It wants to change the slogan of the state from “Think Modern” to “Think German”, and reintroduce the singing of the country’s national anthem in schools.

items: Will the AfD be able to form a state government? Despite its resounding victory, the party fell just short of a majority. It was seeking an absolute majority in the state legislature to govern alone and overcome the so-called “firewall” of the mainstream parties, which refuse to work with it. The final results showed the AfD falling three seats short, with 39 lawmakers in an 83-member legislature.

What has been the reaction in Washington and Moscow? Donald Trump posted a screenshot of the election projection without comment on his Truth Social site. The Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev took a screengrab of Trump’s post and praised a “historic win for the pragmatic AfD”. The AfD is pro-Kremlin, urging a stop to support for Ukraine and pushing for Ukrainians in Germany to no longer receive refugee status.

blocks.text: Iran war likely to drag on for another six months, former US defense secretary warns

blocks.caption: Leon Panetta said the Iran conflict risked becoming another ‘forever war in the Middle East’. Photograph: Paul Buck/EPA

blocks.text: Donald Trump’s war with Iran is likely to drag on for another six months, the former US defense secretary Leon Panetta has said, adding that it risks becoming another “forever war in the Middle East”, with no clear end in sight.

“It’s no mystery that the United States and Iran are caught in a terrible stalemate, in which there really are very few options available to bring this war to an end,” said Panetta, who also served as CIA director under Barack Obama. “I think the likelihood is this war is going to continue for another six months without being resolved,” he added.

items: Who else has been saying Trump’s war may not achieve its aims? The US energy secretary, Chris Wright, said on Sunday morning Washington might not be able to reach an agreement with Tehran that would prevent Iran from having nuclear weapons. “We are strangling their economy to try to bring either a change in policy from the existing regime or a new regime,” he said.

blocks.text: Lindsay Clancy murder trial ends in dramatic deadlock

blocks.caption: The case against Lindsay Clancy has ceased for the moment, but the legal wrangling is not over and a second trial could now be on the horizon. Photograph: Greg Derr/Reuters

blocks.text: Lindsay Clancy, prosecutors, defense lawyers, the judge and the millions watching on were back where they started after her five-week trial over the murder of her three children ended in a mistrial. The case has ceased for the moment, but the legal wrangling is not over and a second trial could now be on the horizon, prolonging and repeating an agonizing spectacle that has gripped the US and the world.

items: What will Clancy’s defense team most likely do? They will almost certainly push to have the charges against their client dropped, aggressively lobby against another trial and make a case to the district attorney’s office along the lines of: “Why are you doing this to this poor woman? She’s still clearly obviously suffering. She’s been punished with her paralysis and, worse than that, the loss of her three children.”

blocks.text: Flock surveillance cameras spur rare bipartisan backlash

blocks.caption: There are about 120,000 Flock cameras across the US, which conduct roughly 2bn scans a month. Photograph: Brian Snyder/Reuters

blocks.text: Growing factions from both sides of the political aisle in the US are pushing back against surveillance cameras made by a single company, a rare response in a sharply divided country with a president pushing an unwaveringly pro-tech agenda.

There are about 120,000 Flock cameras across the US, which conduct roughly 2bn scans a month. The company is staring down controversy after reports of abuses of its cameras by police officers in multiple states, who have used them to stalk former lovers and track people seeking abortions. The network the cameras feed into is also frequently used by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

articles.title: 26 Filipino seafarers awaiting repatriation after Ukraine attack
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines—The 26 Filipino crewmen of the bulk carrier Gingo are awaiting repatriation to the Philippines after safely disembarking following an attack while it was docked in Ukraine, the…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines—The 26 Filipino crewmen of the bulk carrier Gingo are awaiting repatriation to the Philippines after safely disembarking following an attack while it was docked in Ukraine, the Department of Migrant Workers (DMW) said in a statement Monday.
The DMW said that as of Sept. 4, the 26 Filipino seafarers safely disembarked from the vessel. The seafarers are currently awaiting transit to Moldova before their repatriation to the Philippines.

The DMW said it is coordinating with the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA), Philippine Embassy in Warsaw, Philippine Consulate General in Kyiv and Migrant Workers Office (MWO) in Prague to monitor the seafarers’ condition and facilitate their “safe and immediate” return, including the processing of their travel documents with Moldovan authorities and the ship owner.
Labor Attaché Llewelyn Perez said the Philippine diplomatic posts were working with Moldovan authorities and the shipowner to complete the documents needed for the crew’s return.

“The Philippine Embassy and the Philippine Consulate in Kyiv are coordinating with the relevant authorities, in partnership with the shipowner, to facilitate the processing of their travel documents,” Perez said.
The DMW said it is also coordinating with the licensed manning agency and the ship owner to address the seafarers’ immediate needs following their disembarkation.

“The DMW assures the families of the affected seafarers that it, together with its MWOs, Philippine embassies, and consulates, is facilitating the necessary arrangements for their safe return to the Philippines.” /gsg

articles.title: Kenya minister warns foreigners against 'misusing' visas to trade
articles.summary: Kenya is due to start enforcing measures to restrict foreign nationals from operating small-scale businesses.

blocks.text: Kenya's trade ministry has warned foreign nationals that visa-free entry into the country does not grant them the right to work, as the government vows to shut down unlicensed small businesses run by foreigners.
President William Ruto had set today as the deadline for foreigners operating small-scale businesses to cease work.
Ahead of the move, the Burundian embassy in Kenya said it would offer emergency free travel documents to its citizens willing to go back home, amid reports of the mistreatment of Burundians.
It is unclear how many foreign nationals are involved in small-scale trading or how many would be affected by the crackdown.

In a statement, the trade ministry said there was a "deliberate misuse of visa applications by some visitors", adding that some entered Kenya as investors or tourists but then got involved in business activities in breach of their declared status.

"Owing to the high number of foreigners involved in the retail and local trade sectors, there is therefore a need to align their activities and ensure compliance with work permit provisions," Trade Minister Lee Kinyanjui said.
Last week, Ruto said that Kenya remained open to foreign investment, but it could not be "that a person comes from China or elsewhere to be a hawker or open a small shop".
He argued that investors should create jobs and expand production rather than compete with Kenyans in small businesses.
Ruto's comments sparked mixed reactions, with some critics describing them as a populist move that risked stoking xenophobia. Government officials deny the allegation.
Burundi's Foreign Affairs Minister Edouard Bizimana said in a post on X that "Kenyans in Burundi were living peacefully but if the hate speech against Burundi continues things will certainty change".
"Kenya government is responsible for the lives of Burundians living in Kenya," he added.
Bizimana's post followed an urgent meeting he held with representatives of the East African Community (EAC), an eight-member bloc which promotes economic integration in the region.
Both Kenya and Burundi are part of the group. Kenyan representatives attended the meeting called by Bizimana in Burundi.
Bizimana said he had asked the Kenyan ambassador to convey to his government Burundi's concerns and to ensure that no Burundian was subjected to abuse.
On Sunday, a top official in Kenya's foreign affairs ministry said foreigners, with the required documentation, including "work permits and licences", could continue their activities.

"Burundian nationals and all East Africans - and Africans for that matter - are free to live in Kenya as long as they conduct their businesses or work according to the requirements of our laws, Permanent Secretary Korir Sing'oei said.
The government's clarification, however, did little to ease concerns among some foreign traders.
Alexis Ntinanirwa, the head of the Association of Burundians living in Kenya, told the BBC Great Lakes service that he was unhappy with Ruto's decision, but was urging Burundians to remain patient.
He warned that the issue could have wider regional consequences because Kenyans are also involved in small-scale businesses in other East African countries.

"This issue is not only going to cause problems for Burundians working in Kenya, but it is also going to cause problems in the region because there are also Kenyans doing these small jobs in our countries in Burundi, Tanzania and Uganda."
Ntinanirwa advised Burundians involved in hawking and other small businesses to avoid confrontation with police.
Additional reporting by Akisa Wandera and Prime Ndikumagenge

articles.title: Russia opens first road bridge with North Korea
articles.summary: Russia and North Korea have opened their first road bridge across the Tumen River as political, economic and military ties between the two countries deepen.

image.caption: The new Russia-North Korea road bridge is named after Soviet Red Army officer Yakov Novichenko, who is credited with saving North Korean founder Kim Il Sung's lifeImage: Yuri Smityuk/TASS/picture alliance

blocks.text: Russia and North Korea on Monday cut the ribbon on the first road bridge linking the two countries as Moscow and Pyongyang deepen their strategic partnership.
The crossing spans the Tumen River and marks another expansion of transport links between the two countries.
Where is the new bridge?
The road crossing is near the existing Friendship Bridge, a railway bridge commissioned in 1959 following the Korean War.
Russia and North Korea already have direct rail and air connections, but until now there had been no road bridge between them.
The new bridge is named after Soviet Red Army officer Yakov Novichenko, who is credited with saving North Korean founder Kim Il Sung's life. Relatives of Novichenko attended the opening ceremony.

blocks.caption: Nikolai Shcherbitsky and Tatyana Shcherbitskaya joined the ceremony to unveil the bridge named after their grandfather and father respectivelyImage: Yuri Smityuk/TASS/picture alliance

blocks.text: Construction began in April 2025 after the project was agreed during Russian President Vladimir Putin's visit to North Korea in 2024.
Why is the road bridge being opened now?
Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin said the new crossing should boost economic development, tourism and employment.

"I am convinced that the expansion of cross-border transport infrastructure will provide a powerful impetus for the further development of trade, economic, scientific, technological and cultural cooperation," the TASS news agency quoted Mishustin as saying by video link at the opening ceremony.
Relations between Moscow and Pyongyang have strengthened considerably since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
North Korea sent thousands of troops to Russia's Kursk region to help Russian forces repel a Ukrainian incursion launched in 2024.

articles.title: Germany's far-right AfD says 'democracy demands' parties work with them after state election win
articles.summary: The far-right party is trying to form a government in the state after falling three seats short of a majority.

blocks.text: The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is "very, very close" to taking power, its deputy parliamentary leader has told the BBC, after a historic victory in elections for the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.
Sunday's preliminary results show it fell three seats short of an outright majority, with 43.8% of the vote. It is now seeking support from other parties or individuals in order to govern.
While most German political parties refuse to work with the AfD, Beatrix von Storch called for its opponents to enter talks and said: "You cannot say I do not accept the vote of the people".
No far-right party has controlled a German state since World War Two, and governing at state level would mean powers over policing and local education.
Von Storch said if parties refused to work with the AfD, "then we might end up in severe chaos and maybe we have a new election".
Her comments were echoed by AfD's leader in Saxony-Anhalt, Ulrich Siegmund, who told a news conference on Monday that the party had won a "clear mandate to govern".
Saxony-Anhalt has a small population of 2.1 million and the AfD in the state is assessed by domestic intelligence as "right-wing extremist", a classification rejected by Siegmund, 35.
Siegmund said discussions with other parties were initiated on Sunday night and could potentially take days or weeks to conclude.
"We reach out to everybody first, we will have consultations and then we'll see whether [there are] individual parliamentary groups or MPs who would be willing to help us," he added.
The AfD is currently heading for 39 seats in the 83-seat state parliament instead of the 42 needed for an outright majority, although the result has not yet been finalised.

Von Storch told the BBC the AfD was talking to individuals within the conservative CDU group - the largest party in both the state's outgoing coalition and Germany's government - because they were "very, very unhappy with their own party".
In Saxony-Anhalt, the CDU won 17.2% of the vote, according to preliminary results.
One idea being floated is whether there could be informal deal whereby a small party - the BSW - could give their tacit support to allow the AfD to form a minority government.
The left-wing populist BSW, which is set to win five seats, is also tough on migration and backs importing Russian gas.
The AfD has signalled an openness to talk with other parties but all - apart from the BSW - refuse to co-operate with the far-right.
The AfD leads the opinion polls nationally, ahead of the ruling conservatives of Chancellor Friedrich Merz and the Social Democrats, but their heartland lies in the eastern states.
They also won the 2024 state election in neighbouring Thuringia, but failed to secure enough seats to win power.

Among the AfD's policies is a highly controversial plan for "remigration", which is widely understood to mean mass deportations of migrants, although the party says it refers to deporting criminals and those in the country illegally.

articles.title: Russia and North Korea open first road bridge across their shared border
articles.summary:
Connection across Tumen River is further sign of closer ties between the two countries since start of war in Ukraine

Russia and North Korea have opened

blocks.text: Russia and North Korea have opened the first road bridge across their shared border, in the latest sign of the rapidly deepening ties between the two countries since the start of the war in Ukraine.

The one-kilometre bridge spans the Tumen River between Khasan in Russia’s far east and Tumangang in North Korea, along a remote and sparsely populated stretch of the countries’ shared border just a few miles from the coast.

Speaking by video link during the bridge’s opening ceremony on Monday, Russia’s prime minister, Mikhail Mishustin, said the new crossing would spur development in a range of areas, including tourism, while creating new jobs

“I am convinced that the expansion of cross-border transport infrastructure will provide a powerful impetus for the further development of trade, economic, scientific, technological and cultural cooperation,” Mishustin said.
The road bridge is named after the Soviet officer Yakov Novichenko, who is credited with saving North Korea’s founding leader, Kim Il-sung, from an assassination attempt by a pro-South Korean group.
After the opening ceremony, convoys of vehicles crossed the bridge from both sides.
Russia and the secretive North Korea regime are already connected by a railway bridge across the Tumen, as well as regular flights between Vladivostok and Pyongyang.
Ukrainian human rights groups have warned that the bridge may be intended to provide a discreet military logistics corridor between the two countries.

Truth Hounds, a Ukrainian human rights organisation, has described it as a likely future corridor for moving North Korean troops, construction brigades and military officials into Russia, while allowing Russian technology and resources to travel in the opposite direction with less risk of detection.

Ties between Moscow and Pyongyang have strengthened dramatically since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. North Korea has sent thousands of troops to Russia’s Kursk region to help Moscow repel a Ukrainian incursion launched there in 2024.
In return, Russia is believed to have provided North Korea with air-defence missiles, electronic warfare equipment, drones and spy-satellite technology, according to South Korean intelligence.

Russian and North Korean officials have also touted North Korea as a new holiday destination since the country reopened to Russian tourists in 2024, with thousands of Russians visiting its newly opened beach resorts and ski slopes since then.
Russia’s increasingly close embrace of totalitarian North Korea has raised eyebrows even in Moscow.

During an interview with the Russian broadcaster RBC last month, a reporter asked Sergei Lavrov, Russia’s longtime foreign minister, how the country had “ended up” with just “two allies – North Korea and Iran”.
Lavrov pushed back against the premise, saying there was “nothing wrong” with such company.
At the same time, some of Russia’s traditional partners have shown growing frustration with Moscow’s continuing war in Ukraine and the fallout it has caused across the region.

During a meeting in July, Kazakhstan’s president, Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, a longtime ally of Moscow, told the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, that he was hearing from leaders of many countries who questioned why Russia was still waging the war.
“The nature of the conflict isn’t entirely clear for many, including us,” Tokayev told Putin.

articles.title: Nepal observes national day of mourning for victims of flash flood disaster
articles.summary: Flags flew at half mast on the 13th day since the disaster, the last day of the Hindu mourning period.

blocks.text: Nepalis observed a national day of mourning for the victims of the flash flood on Monday, lighting candles to mark the last day of the traditional 13-day Hindu mourning period.
While flags were flown at half mast, commemorations were scaled back as rescue teams continue to search for survivors. Candlelight vigils were planned for Monday evening.

At least 1,287 people are known to have died after a flash flood, believed to have been triggered by a glacial collapse, swept through villages in a Himalayan valley along border between Nepal and Tibet.
Almost two weeks later, more than 5,000 people are still missing.

Phanindra Paudel of the National Emergency Operation Centre (NEOC) told the Reuters news agency that there would be "no government programmes organised as the rescue and search operation is still going on in the flood-hit areas."
Nepal's president, Ram Chandra Paudel, toured areas devastated by the floods on Monday, an aide told Reuters.
The home ministry said that government offices, as well as missions abroad, would fly the national flag at half mast to mark the final day of the mourning period.

Australian tunnel rescue expert Arnold Dix, who is advising Nepali teams, said in an update on X that the operation meant facing "multiple potential rescues, unfolding at the same time, in different places, each with its own dangers, uncertainties and lives that may still be saved."
Four people have been rescued in recent days, three at hydropower stations or tunnels.
On Saturday, a 64-year-old Nepali woman was pulled from her buried house on Saturday, more than 10 days after a wall of ice, rock and mud partially buried her house in the Nuwakot district.
She was discovered alive on the fourth floor of the building by Nepal's Armed Police Force and airlifted to a hospital in Kathmandu for treatment.
On Sunday rescue workers in China recovered twelve bodies in the Nepal-Tibet border, using excavators, shovels and ground penetrating radar at the site.
At least 5,083 people are still missing in Nepal. On the Tibetan side, the death toll reported by Chinese media on Friday was 31, with 531 people unaccounted for.

articles.title: Israeli strikes on southern Lebanese town kill 11, state news agency says
articles.summary: Israeli strikes on a southern Lebanese town early on Monday killed at least 11 people including two children and two medics, Lebanon's state news agency said.

image.caption: Rescue workers search for victims under the rubble of a building destroyed in an Israeli airstrike in the southern village of Kfar Rumman, Lebanon, on Monday. (Mohammed Zaatari/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World
Israeli strikes on a southern Lebanese town early on Monday killed at least 11 people including two children and two medics, Lebanon's state news agency said.
2 children were killed in the airstrike on the town of Kfar Rumman, news report says

Israel has intensified its bombardment of south Lebanon in recent days despite a June ceasefire that was meant to halt fighting between the Israeli military and Lebanese armed group Hezbollah. At least seven people were killed in Israeli strikes on Sunday.
Just after midnight, Israeli warplanes hit a residential building in the town of Kfar Rumman in southern Lebanon, killing nine people including two children, Lebanon's National News Agency reported.
A separate Israeli drone strike on a civilian vehicle in the town killed two medics inside the car, it said.

According to The Associated Press, Lebanon's Health Ministry said one of the strikes hit a building, killing eight people — including a child and two women. It added that 11 people were also wounded, including four children and two women.
No evacuation warning

The strikes on the town came without an online evacuation warning from the Israeli military. The Israeli military did not immediately respond to Reuters' questions on the strikes, including whether it was aware of the presence of medics and children at the strike locations and why no evacuation warning was issued.

A spokesperson for the Israeli military issued a separate evacuation warning just after 2:00 a.m. local time for areas around a building in another town in southern Lebanon where it said it would strike Hezbollah facilities.

items: Israeli strikes kill 4 in southern Lebanon

blocks.text: Israeli strikes on Lebanon have killed more than 4,300 people since Hezbollah launched rockets at Israel on March 2 — two days after the start of U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran — triggering an Israeli air and ground offensive.
The ceasefire saw violence decrease dramatically, but Israeli troops occupying swathes of southern Lebanon have continued razing villages in the self-declared security zone.
Israel's military has continued carrying out strikes both within the zone and to its north, mostly without evacuation warnings.

September 7, 2026
Zelenskyy says Russian drone targeted SBU chief's office

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Monday that a Russian drone which struck the headquarters of Ukraine's SBU security service in Kyiv on Friday had been aimed directly at the office of the agency's chief.
The revelation adds to the significance of one of the most high-profile Russian strikes on a Ukrainian government building since the start of the full-scale invasion.
SBU chief Oleksandr Poklad was not there at the time and was unharmed.
Zelenskyy said he had instructed the SBU to prepare an "appropriate, tangible response" and suggested Ukraine could retaliate in a similar manner.
Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha called the strike a "major escalation."
Black smoke was seen rising from the SBU building, close to the UNESCO-listed St. Sophia Cathedral.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said at least 12 people were wounded in the wider attack on the capital, although it was not immediately clear whether any of them were injured at the SBU headquarters.
The strike also damaged nearby buildings and shattered windows in the area.
It was the first time the SBU headquarters had been hit since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.

The SBU plays a central role in Ukraine's war effort and has carried out long-range and covert operations against Russian military targets. It was behind Operation Spiderweb in 2025, when drones targeted Russian strategic bombers at air bases deep inside Russia, as well as the 2022 bombing of the bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea.

articles.title: Weather tracker: Typhoon Saudel causes mass evacuations in south-east China
articles.summary:
Torrential rain causes widespread damage; while north-west South Africa hit by thunderstorms and central-southern US faces oppressive heat

Typhoon Saudel brought days of torrential rain to…

blocks.text: Typhoon Saudel brought days of torrential rain to the Zhejiang, Jiangxi, Fujian and Guangdong provinces in south-east China last week. The city of Putian, in Fujian province, recorded 416.5mm of rain in a 24-hour period between Thursday and Friday, with surrounding villages recording more than 500mm in the same period. In Fujian, authorities estimate that almost 600,000 people were evacuated from high-risk, flood-prone areas. A further 128,000 people in 53 counties were also affected across Jiangxi, with emergency evacuations affecting 9,000 people.

Flooding, landslips and infrastructure damage were reported widely in the region. More than 2,500 teachers and students were trapped in a school compound in the Zhejiang city of Wenzhou on Wednesday after extreme rainfall caused flash floods in low-lying areas. At least 1,260 people reportedly had to be rescued in Putian after a river embankment collapsed on Thursday, flattening 100 homes. On Saturday, a landslip in a village of Suichuan county, in Jiangxi province, killed three people and nine others remaining missing.
This is the seventh typhoon to affect China this year, and Saudel arrived shortly after Typhoon Narra dumped heavy rain on Guangdong, Hainan and Guangxi late last month.

The South African Weather Service implemented several thunderstorm warnings late last week, covering a large swathe of the northern and western provinces. Disruptive rainfall, damaging winds, excessive lightning and hail were all reported, with rainfall totals expected to have reached at least 75-100mm for parts of the Northern Cape and North West provinces over the weekend. In Johannesburg, eight families were evacuated from an apartment building after strong winds tore off a significant part of its roof.

Oppressive heat in the US affected states across the central-southern plains and the Mississippi valley this weekend, with maximum temperatures easily reaching the high 30s (Celsius; high 90s Fahrenheit). However, with high humidities, the heat indices in this region have been closer to 40-43C (105–110F). The unrelenting temperatures will continue across the midwest and southern US this week, with maximum temperatures continuing to reach the high 30s.

articles.title: UK government condemns 'thuggish' anti-migrant protests in Portsmouth
articles.summary: Hundreds gathered in Portsmouth after some refugees arrived by boat from France, a day after masked protesters disrupted traffic at the port of Dover.

image.caption: Hundreds of protesters gathered in Portsmouth following the arrival of about migrants who had crossed the English Channel from FranceImage: PA/PA Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: Britishminister Emma Reynolds on Monday slammed "thuggish" anti-migrant protests that blocked roads in the English coastal city of Portsmouth.
Hundreds of protesters gathered in Portsmouth on Sunday following the arrival of about 140 migrants who had crossed the English Channel from France, UK media reported.
"This is thuggish and intimidating behavior," Reynolds, who is Chief Secretary to the Treasury, told Sky News, adding that the police brought the Portsmouth protest under control.
The demonstration came a day after masked protesters disrupted traffic at Dover terminal, blocking routes to the busy ferry port.
Masked protesters in Dover
On Saturday, hundreds of masked people blocked traffic at England's port of Dover as part of an anti-migrant protest, halting ferry traffic between France and the UK.

Video footage showed demonstrators, reportedly backed by far-right groups, in balaclavas chanting "stop the boats," in a reference to refugees and migrants who attempt the dangerous English Channel crossing in a bid to reach Great Britain.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham's Labour Party government said that "the right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy, but we condemn the behavior in Dover and the travel disruption it has caused."
The Dover demonstration caused a traffic jam of about four miles (6.4 km) and temporarily halted traffic into and out of the port.
Britain has struggled for years to curb small-boat crossings from France, although Reynolds said arrivals were down 43% from last year to about 17,000 so far this year.

articles.title: Minister condemns ‘thuggish’ far-right, anti-migrant protesters in Portsmouth – UK politics live
articles.summary:
Emma Reynolds says demonstrations ‘cross a line’

Good morning. John Healey is giving his first major speech on economic policy since he became chancellor seven weeks ago.…

blocks.text: Minister condemns ‘thuggish’ far-right, anti-migrant protesters in Portsmouth

Good morning. John Healey is giving his first major speech on economic policy since he became chancellor seven weeks ago. It is meant to be the main government news of the morning and, as Pippa Crerar writes in her preview story, Healey will argue the government’s plans to boost growth across the whole country will enable the British economy to “turn a corner”.
Healey’s deputy, Emma Reynolds, the chief secretary to the Treasury, has been giving interviews as part of the build-up.

But, as well as taking questions about growth and tax, Reynolds has also found herself taking questions about the latest far-right protest about immigration, triggered by a large boat carrying migrants arriving for the first time in Portsmouth.
Commenting on the behaviour of the protesters, who blocked roads and some of whom were masked, Reynolds said:

double quotation markThis is thuggish and intimidating behaviour. This is not peaceful protest. Obviously, as a politician, I absolutely support people’s right to peaceful protest. But this crosses a line and I just want to take the opportunity to thank the police and other emergency services who have brought this under control. We do not want to see this kind of behaviour anywhere, frankly.
Here is the agenda for the day.
Around 9.30am: John Healey, the chancellor, gives a speech on economic growth in the West Midlands.
11.30am: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.
2.30pm: Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, takes questions in the Commons.
After 3.30pm: Emma Reynolds, the chief secretary to the Treasury, is due to make a statement to MPs.
Afternoon: MPs start debating the remaining stages of the health bill.
And Chris Bryant, the Northern Ireland secretary, is today meeting the Northern Ireland political leaders, as MLAs (members of the legislative assembly) return to Stormont after the summer recess.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

blocks.text: Healey says he wants growth story 'written in more places'
John Healey is about to deliver his speech on the economy. Here are extracts that were released overnight by the Treasury.
On the UK turning the corner

double quotation markA new story about Britain. An optimistic story. One of resilience. Pride. Huge latent potential. A country turning a corner. A country whose people, businesses and communities are ready to seize the opportunity of new technologies and new ideas.
On what makes good growth

double quotation markAsk an economist what growth is and you’ll get a number. But ask the country and you’ll get a different answer. A young person getting a new job in a company that’s on the up. A sole trader winning a new contract that pays for a holiday with their kids. A business winning a new export order, giving the community around it a new lease of life.” The prime minister laid out a clear diagnosis of what has gone wrong in the past. The solution is a fundamental shift that starts with putting power in the right places. The next chapter of Britain’s growth story will be written in more places.
On the importance of wealth creation

double quotation markInstead of getting in the way with complexity and red tape, we need a strong, strategic centre wired to enable local leaders and their ambitions. That’s why we created No 10 North, working on a dual mission with the Treasury, removing obstacles so that local leaders and businesses can pull together to drive growth and productivity. I want to see wealth creation in this country. I want to see businesses make a profit. And to create the conditions for that we need an active, accountable state at all levels to remove blockages and create the conditions for more investment.
